    PART I. FUNDAMENTALS OF IMMUNOLOGY

    1. The human immune system

    The immune system is an integrated system of cells, tissues, organs, and soluble substances responsible for protecting the body against foreign substances and infectious agents.

    Important terminology

    TermDefinitionImportant distinction
    ImmunityAbility to resist infection or foreign substancesOverall protective capacity
    ImmunologyStudy of immune responsesStudy of the immune system
    AntigenSubstance recognized by the immune systemNot all antigens necessarily produce an immune response
    ImmunogenSubstance capable of inducing an immune responseAll immunogens are antigens, but not all antigens are immunogens
    AntibodyImmunoglobulin produced by B cells/plasma cells in response to antigenic stimulationSpecifically binds an antigen
    Cellular immunityImmune response primarily mediated by cellsMainly T lymphocytes
    Humoral immunityImmune response mediated by antibodies and soluble factorsMainly B lymphocytes and antibodies

    Two major components of immunity

    Cellular immunityHumoral immunity
    Involves immune cellsInvolves antibodies and soluble mediators
    Primarily mediated by T lymphocytesPrimarily mediated by B lymphocytes and plasma cells
    Important against intracellular pathogens, infected cells and tumor cellsImportant against extracellular microorganisms and toxins
    Includes cytotoxic T-cell activityIncludes antibody neutralization, opsonization and complement activation

    2. Categories of immunity

    There are two major categories:

    • Innate immunity – natural, nonspecific immunity.
    • Adaptive immunity – acquired, antigen-specific immunity.

    Innate versus adaptive immunity

    CharacteristicInnate immunityAdaptive immunity
    SpecificityNonspecificAntigen-specific
    OnsetImmediate or rapidSlower during initial exposure
    MemoryNo classical antigen-specific memoryHas immunologic memory
    ReceptorsGermline-encoded pattern recognition receptorsB-cell receptors and T-cell receptors
    Response upon repeated exposureGenerally similarFaster and stronger
    Major componentsSkin, mucosa, complement, phagocytes, NK cellsB cells, T cells, antibodies
    Main functionFirst-line defenseSpecific and sustained protection

    EXAM TIP: Innate immunity acts first. Adaptive immunity provides specificity and immunologic memory.

    A. Innate immunity

    The source identifies the following characteristics:

    1. Functions during the early stages of host defense.
    2. Its magnitude and effectiveness are generally not altered by previous exposure to the same foreign agent.
    3. Includes anatomical barriers, resident flora, hereditary influences, cellular factors and humoral factors.

    Anatomical and physical barriers

    BarrierProtective mechanism
    SkinPhysical barrier that prevents microbial entry
    CiliaMove mucus and trapped microorganisms out of respiratory passages
    MucusTraps microorganisms and foreign particles
    Gastric acidDestroys many ingested microorganisms
    EarwaxTraps particles and contains antimicrobial substances
    SecretionsMay contain enzymes and antimicrobial molecules
    TearsWash away microorganisms; contain lysozyme

    Resident flora / microbiota

    Normal microbiota prevent pathogen multiplication through colonization resistance.

    They accomplish this by:

    • Competing for nutrients.
    • Occupying attachment sites.
    • Producing antimicrobial substances.
    • Modifying the local environment.

    Examples from the reviewer:

    SiteExamples
    Oral cavityViridans streptococci
    IntestinesNormal gram-negative anaerobic bacilli and other commensals
    SkinStaphylococcus epidermidis
    VaginaLactobacillus acidophilus

    Remember: Normal microbiota protect against pathogens, but disruption of normal flora can allow opportunistic infections.

    Hereditary and genetic influences

    Genetic differences influence susceptibility to infection and immune responses.

    Examples:

    • Interracial or individual genetic differences.
    • Blood group phenotypes and antigens.
    • Duffy-null phenotype and resistance to certain Plasmodium vivax strains.
    • HLA inheritance and disease susceptibility.

    Cellular factors: WBCs

    The following cells are particularly important in innate immunity.

    Comprehensive WBC comparison table

    CellNormal proportion of WBCs (approx.)MorphologyMain functionImportant associations
    Neutrophils40–70%Multilobed nucleus, fine granulesPhagocytosis; first responders in acute bacterial infectionNeutrophilia in bacterial infection
    Eosinophils1–4%Bilobed nucleus, large orange-red granulesDefense against parasites; allergic responsesParasitic infection, asthma, allergies
    Basophils0–1%Dark blue-purple granules obscure nucleusRelease histamine and heparinType I hypersensitivity
    Lymphocytes20–40%Large round nucleus, scant cytoplasmAdaptive immunity and NK-cell activityViral infections, lymphoproliferative disorders
    Monocytes2–8%Large cell, kidney- shaped nucleusPhagocytosis; differentiate into macrophagesChronic infections and inflammation

    High-yield distinctions:

    • Neutrophils: Most abundant circulating WBC; increased in acute bacterial infections.
    • Eosinophils: Parasites and allergies.
    • Basophils: Histamine and heparin.
    • Monocytes: Largest circulating WBC; become tissue macrophages.
    • Lymphocytes: B cells, T cells and NK cells.

    Tissue macrophages

    Monocytes migrate from the blood into tissues and differentiate into macrophages.

    Tissue / organMacrophage name
    LiverKupffer cells
    Connective tissueHistiocytes
    Brain / CNSMicroglial cells
    LungsAlveolar macrophages / dust cells
    Lymph nodesLymph node macrophages
    SpleenSplenic macrophages
    BoneOsteoclasts
    PlacentaHofbauer cells

    Memory aid: Kupffer = liver; microglia = brain; dust cells = lungs.

    3. Phagocytosis

    Phagocytosis is the process by which phagocytic cells engulf and destroy microorganisms, particles, and cellular debris.

    The source attributes the classical description of phagocytosis to Élie Metchnikoff (1888– 1900).

    Five major stages of phagocytosis

    StageProcessExplanation
    1. InitiationTissue damage or infection triggers the responseSignals attract phagocytes
    2. ChemotaxisDirected movement toward a chemical stimulusPhagocytes migrate to the infection site
    3. Recognition and attachmentAntigen recognitionPhagocyte binds the microorganism
    4. EngulfmentFormation of pseudopods and phagosomeOrganism is internalized
    5. DigestionPhagolysosome formationEnzymes and reactive substances destroy the organism

    Chemotaxis

    Chemotaxis is the directed movement of cells in response to chemical signals.

    TypeMeaning
    Positive chemotaxisMovement toward the chemical stimulus
    Negative chemotaxisMovement away from the chemical stimulus
    Random movementMovement without a directional chemical stimulus

    Important chemotactic substances include:

    • C5a – powerful complement-derived chemotactic factor.
    • C3a – inflammatory mediator; less potent as a chemoattractant than C5a.
    • IL-8 (CXCL8) – recruits neutrophils.
    • Bacterial products and other inflammatory mediators.

    Disorders of phagocyte movement

    DisorderDefectMain consequence
    Job syndrome (Hyper-IgE syndrome)Impaired neutrophil chemotaxis associated with STAT3 dysfunction in classic diseaseRecurrent infections, eczema, elevated IgE
    Lazy leukocyte syndromeImpaired chemotaxis and random migrationRecurrent bacterial infections
    Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)Defective NADPH oxidase and respiratory burstRecurrent catalase-positive infections
    Chediak-Higashi syndromeDefective lysosomal traffickingImpaired phagolysosome function, recurrent infections

    Important differentiation: Job syndrome and CGD are not the same. Job syndrome is classically associated with defective Th17-related immunity and impaired neutrophil recruitment, while CGD is associated with defective oxidative killing.

    Recognition of microorganisms

    There are two major mechanisms:

    1. Direct recognition through pattern recognition receptors (PRRs)

    • PRRs recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs).
    • PAMPs are conserved microbial structures.
    • Examples include bacterial lipopolysaccharide and other microbial components.

    2. Indirect recognition through opsonization

    Opsonins coat microorganisms, making them easier for phagocytes to engulf.

    OpsoninFunction
    IgGBinds Fc receptors on phagocytes
    C3bBinds complement receptors
    C-reactive protein (CRP)Promotes recognition and complement-related opsonization

    Remember: Opsonization = coating the microorganism to facilitate phagocytosis.

    Digestion and microbial killing

    After engulfment, the phagosome fuses with lysosomes to form a phagolysosome.

    Microbial killing involves:

    • Lysozyme – breaks bacterial peptidoglycan.
    • Lactoferrin – binds iron, limiting microbial growth.
    • Defensins – disrupt microbial membranes.
    • Reactive oxygen species – superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radicals.
    • Other lysosomal enzymes.

    Respiratory burst: Rapid production of reactive oxygen species following phagocyte activation.

    4. Natural killer cells (NK cells)

    NK cells are large granular lymphocytes responsible for innate immune defense against virus-infected cells and tumor cells.

    CharacteristicNK cells
    OriginLymphoid lineage
    ImmunityInnate
    CD markersCD16 and CD56
    T-cell receptorAbsent
    B-cell receptorAbsent
    Main targetsVirus-infected and malignant cells
    Killing mechanismPerforin and granzymes
    Antibody-dependent killingADCC through CD16

    Mechanism of NK-cell killing

    1. NK cell recognizes an abnormal or infected target.
    2. Perforin forms pores in the target-cell membrane.
    3. Granzymes enter the cell.
    4. Granzymes activate apoptotic pathways.
    5. The target cell undergoes apoptosis.

    High-yield: NK cells are CD16+, CD56+, CD3− in their conventional phenotype.

    5. Antigen-presenting cells (APCs)

    APCs process antigens and present antigen-derived peptides to T lymphocytes through MHC molecules.

    Major APCs

    APCImportant function
    Dendritic cellsMost effective professional APCs for activating naïve T cells
    MacrophagesPhagocytose pathogens and present antigens
    B lymphocytesBind specific antigens and present processed peptides

    Specialized dendritic cells

    CellLocation
    Langerhans cellsSkin and mucosal epithelium
    Interstitial dendritic cellsHeart, lungs, liver, kidneys and GI tract
    Interdigitating dendritic cellsLymphoid tissues, especially T-cell areas

    MHC class I versus MHC class II

    FeatureMHC class IMHC class II
    DistributionAlmost all nucleated cellsProfessional APCs
    Antigen sourceEndogenous / intracellularExogenous / extracellular
    Presents toCD8+ T cellsCD4+ T cells
    Main functionIdentifies infected or abnormal cellsActivates helper T-cell responses
    HLA moleculesHLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-CHLA-DP, HLA-DQ, HLA-DR

    Memory aid:

    • Class I → CD8 → cytotoxic.
    • Class II → CD4 → helper.

    6. Humoral factors: cytokines, chemokines and acute-phase reactants

    These soluble substances regulate inflammation, immune-cell activity and host defense.

    Cytokines

    Cytokines are signaling proteins that allow immune cells to communicate.

    High-yield cytokine comparison table

    CytokineMain functionImportant association
    IL-1Induces fever and inflammationEndogenous pyrogen
    IL-2Promotes T-cell proliferationT-cell growth factor
    IL-4Promotes Th2 differentiation and IgE class switchingAllergic responses
    IL-5Stimulates eosinophil growth and activationParasitic infections
    IL-6Stimulates hepatic production of acute-phase proteinsIncreased CRP
    IL-8 (CXCL8)Neutrophil chemotaxisRecruitment of neutrophils
    IL-10Anti-inflammatory; suppresses inflammatory responsesImmune regulation
    IL-12Promotes NK-cell activity and Th1 differentiationCell-mediated immunity
    IL-17Recruits neutrophils and promotes inflammationTh17-mediated immunity
    TNF-αInflammation, fever and endothelial activationSeptic shock in excessive systemic release
    IFN-α / IFN- βAntiviral defenseType I interferons
    IFN-γActivates macrophagesTh1 and cell-mediated immunity
    TGF-βImmunoregulation and tissue repairRegulatory T cells

    Chemokines

    Chemokines are a specialized family of cytokines that primarily direct leukocyte migration.

    ChemokineMain target / role
    CXCL8 (IL-8)Neutrophil recruitment
    CCL2 (MCP-1)Monocyte recruitment
    CCL5 (RANTES)Recruitment of T cells, eosinophils and other leukocytes
    CXCL10 (IP-10)Recruitment of activated T cells
    CXCL12 (SDF-1)Hematopoietic-cell trafficking and homing

    Cytokines versus chemokines: All chemokines are cytokines, but not all cytokines are chemokines. Chemokines specialize in directing cell movement.

    Acute-phase reactants

    Acute-phase reactants are plasma proteins whose concentrations change in response to inflammation, infection or tissue injury.

    Positive acute-phase reactantMain significance
    C-reactive protein (CRP)Opsonization; inflammation marker
    Serum amyloid A (SAA)Inflammation marker
    FibrinogenIncreases ESR
    HaptoglobinBinds free hemoglobin
    α1-antitrypsinProtease inhibitor
    α1-acid glycoproteinInflammatory response
    Complement proteinsEnhance host defense
    FerritinIncreases during inflammation

    Negative acute-phase reactants:

    • Albumin Transferrin Transthyretin (prealbumin)

    These generally decrease during significant inflammation.

    EXAM TIP: CRP is a positive acute-phase reactant; albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant.

    7. Inflammation

    Inflammation is the body's cellular and vascular response to injury, infection or tissue damage.

    Cardinal signs of inflammation

    SignMeaningMechanism
    CalorHeatIncreased blood flow
    RuborRednessVasodilation
    TumorSwellingIncreased vascular permeability
    DolorPainInflammatory mediators and tissue pressure
    Functio laesaLoss of functionTissue damage and swelling

    Stages / outcomes of inflammation

    1. Recognition of injury or pathogen.
    2. Release of inflammatory mediators.
    3. Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.
    4. Leukocyte recruitment and activation.
    5. Elimination of the offending agent.
    6. Resolution, repair or chronic inflammation.

    Possible outcomes:

    • Complete repair and restoration of function.
    • Abscess formation.
    • Granuloma formation.
    • Chronic inflammation and fibrosis.

    8. Adaptive immunity

    Adaptive immunity develops following exposure to a specific antigen.

    Characteristics

    • Antigen specificity.
    • Immunologic memory.
    • Diversity of antigen recognition.
    • Self-tolerance.
    • Clonal expansion of antigen-specific lymphocytes.

    T cells versus B cells

    FeatureT lymphocytesB lymphocytes
    MaturationThymusBone marrow
    Main functionCell-mediated immunityHumoral immunity
    ReceptorT-cell receptor (TCR)B-cell receptor (surface immunoglobulin)
    Antigen recognitionProcessed peptide presented by MHCCan recognize native antigen
    DifferentiationHelper, cytotoxic, regulatory, memoryPlasma cells and memory B cells
    Main productsCytokines / cytotoxic mediatorsAntibodies

    T-cell maturation

    The reviewer identifies these stages:

    StageCD4CD8
    Double negative−−
    Double positive++
    Single positive+ or −− or +

    During maturation, developing T cells undergo selection to establish self-MHC restriction and self-tolerance.

    • Positive selection: T cells must recognize self-MHC.
    • Negative selection: Strongly self-reactive T cells are eliminated.

    Mature T-cell subsets

    T-cell subsetMarkerFunction
    Helper T cellsCD3+, CD4+Coordinate immune responses through cytokines
    Cytotoxic T cellsCD3+, CD8+Destroy infected and malignant cells
    Regulatory T cellsCD4+, CD25+, FOXP3+Suppress excessive immune responses
    Memory T cellsCD3+Rapid response upon re-exposure

    Important: CD25 is the IL-2 receptor α-chain. It is expressed on activated T cells and is also characteristically expressed by regulatory T cells.

    B-cell maturation

    StageCharacteristic
    Pro-B cellEarly B-cell development; CD19+, CD34+ may be present
    Pre-B cellCytoplasmic μ heavy chain; pre-B-cell receptor
    Immature B cellSurface IgM
    Mature naïve B cellSurface IgM and IgD
    Activated B cellAntigen-stimulated; undergoes clonal expansion
    Plasma cellProduces and secretes antibodies
    Memory B cellRapid antibody response after re-exposure

    Plasma cells: Have abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and a prominent perinuclear Golgi zone, reflecting their high antibody-production activity.

    B-cell versus T-cell mitogens

    MitogenMain lymphocyte stimulated
    Lipopolysaccharide (LPS)B cells
    Phytohemagglutinin (PHA)T cells
    Concanavalin A (ConA)T cells
    Pokeweed mitogen (PWM)Both B and T cells

    Activators of lymphocytes

    ActivatorEffect
    AntigensMonoclonal activation of antigen-specific lymphocyte clones
    SuperantigensPolyclonal / nonspecific T-cell activation through MHC II and TCR Vβ interactions
    MitogensPolyclonal activation of lymphocytes

    9. Lymphoid tissues

    Primary versus secondary lymphoid organs

    Primary lymphoid organsSecondary lymphoid organs
    Bone marrowLymph nodes
    ThymusSpleen
    Tonsils
    Peyer's patches
    Appendix
    MALT

    Functions

    Thymus

    • Site of T-cell maturation.
    • Located in the anterior mediastinum.
    • Undergoes involution with age.

    Bone marrow

    • Site of hematopoiesis.
    • Site of B-cell maturation.

    Lymph nodes

    • Filter lymph.
    • Contain antigen-presenting cells and lymphocytes.
    • Important sites of adaptive immune activation.

    Spleen

    • Filters blood.
    • Removes aged and damaged RBCs.
    • Responds to blood-borne antigens.

    MALT

    • Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.
    • Protects mucosal surfaces.

    Lymphocyte laboratory identification

    MethodPrincipleApplication
    Rosette testRBCs bind to lymphocytes bearing specific receptorsHistorical T-cell identification
    Flow cytometryFluorescent antibodies detect cellular markersCD marker identification and immunophenotyping
    Fluorescence microscopyDetects fluorescently labeled cellsVisualization of antigen-antibody binding

    E-rosette test: T lymphocytes bind sheep RBCs through CD2. This is a historical technique; flow cytometry has largely replaced it.

    Ficoll-Hypaque density-gradient centrifugation

    This method separates blood components based on density.

    After centrifugation:

    LayerContents
    TopPlasma
    InterfaceMononuclear cells (lymphocytes and monocytes)
    Ficoll layerDensity-gradient medium
    BottomGranulocytes and erythrocytes

    EXAM TIP: The mononuclear-cell layer is collected from the interface between plasma and Ficoll.

    CD34Hematopoietic stem/progenitor cellsStem-cell marker

    Frequently tested combinations

    CellTypical immunophenotype

    Helper T cellsCD3+, CD4+
    Cytotoxic T cellsCD3+, CD8+
    B cellsCD19+, CD20+
    NK cellsCD16+, CD56+, CD3−

    Remember:

    • CD3 = T cells.
    • CD4 = Helper.

    PART II. ANTIGENS, ANTIBODIES AND COMPLEMENT

    11. Antigens

    An antigen is a substance that can specifically bind to an antibody or antigen receptor of a lymphocyte.

    Antigens may be proteins, carbohydrates, lipids or nucleic acids.

    Important antigen terminology

    TermDefinitionKey point
    AntigenSubstance recognized by an antibody or immune receptorMay or may not induce immunity
    ImmunogenSubstance that induces an immune responseStronger definition than antigen
    EpitopeSpecific portion of an antigen recognized by an antibody or receptorAlso called antigenic determinant
    ParatopeAntigen-binding region of an antibodyLocated in the variable region
    HaptenSmall molecule that cannot induce an immune response independentlyBecomes immunogenic when attached to a carrier
    CarrierLarge molecule attached to a haptenMakes the hapten immunogenic
    AdjuvantSubstance that enhances an immune responseUsed in vaccine preparations

    Monovalent versus multivalent antigens

    Monovalent / univalentMultivalent
    Contains one antigenic determinant of a particular specificityContains multiple antigenic determinants
    Limited antibody-binding opportunitiesCan bind multiple antibody molecules
    Less capable of extensive cross-linkingCan produce lattice formation

    Immunogenicity

    Immunogenicity refers to the ability of a substance to induce an immune response.

    All immunogens are antigens, but not all antigens are immunogens.

    Types of antigens according to origin

    TypeMeaningExamples
    Exogenous antigensEnter the body from outsideBacteria, viruses, fungi, pollen, drugs
    Endogenous antigensOriginate within the bodyIntracellular viral proteins, tumor- associated proteins
    AutoantigensThe individual's own antigensNuclear and cellular proteins
    AlloantigensAntigens from another individual of the same speciesABO, Rh and HLA antigens
    Heteroantigens / xenoantigensAntigens from another speciesAnimal tissue antigens

    Autoantigens and autoimmune diseases

    Autoantigens are self-components that become targets of an inappropriate immune response.

    Autoimmune diseaseImportant autoantibody
    Type 1 diabetes mellitusAnti-islet antibodies, anti-GAD65, IA-2 antibodies
    Pernicious anemiaAnti-intrinsic factor; antiparietal cell antibodies
    Hashimoto thyroiditisAnti-thyroid peroxidase; anti-thyroglobulin
    Graves diseaseTSH receptor-stimulating antibodies
    Multiple sclerosisNo single diagnostic autoantibody; associated with myelin-directed immune responses
    Goodpasture syndromeAnti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies
    Myasthenia gravisAnti-acetylcholine receptor; anti-MuSK in some cases
    Sjögren syndromeAnti-SSA/Ro; anti-SSB/La
    Primary biliary cholangitisAntimitochondrial antibodies
    Chronic active autoimmune hepatitisAnti-smooth muscle; anti-LKM-1 in some types
    Rheumatoid arthritisRheumatoid factor; anti-CCP
    Systemic lupus erythematosusANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith

    High-yield associations:

    • SLE → anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith.
    • Goodpasture → anti-GBM.
    • Graves → TSH receptor-stimulating antibody.
    • Hashimoto → anti-TPO.
    • Myasthenia gravis → anti-AChR.
    • Sjögren → anti-SSA and anti-SSB.
    • Pernicious anemia → anti-intrinsic factor.

    Alloantigens and HLA

    Alloantigens are antigens that differ among individuals belonging to the same species.

    Examples:

    • ABO blood group antigens.
    • Rh antigens.
    • HLA antigens.
    • Other RBC blood group antigens.

    Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) system

    HLA molecules are encoded by genes in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on chromosome 6.

    HLA classMoleculesDistributionPresents to
    Class IHLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-CAlmost all nucleated cellsCD8+ T cells
    Class IIHLA-DP, HLA-DQ, HLA-DRProfessional APCsCD4+ T cells
    Class IIIComplement and inflammatory proteinsVarious tissuesNot classical antigen-presenting molecules

    Clinical significance of HLA

    1. Transplantation: HLA compatibility influences graft acceptance and rejection.
    2. Disease susceptibility: Certain HLA alleles are associated with particular diseases.
    3. Paternity testing: Historically used as a genetic marker, although DNA testing is now preferred.
    4. Platelet transfusion: HLA antibodies can cause platelet refractoriness.
    5. Immunologic identification: Helps distinguish self from non-self.

    Important associations:

    HLA associationDisease
    HLA-B27Ankylosing spondylitis
    HLA-DR3 / DR4Type 1 diabetes mellitus
    HLA-DR4Rheumatoid arthritis
    HLA-DR2Associated with certain autoimmune conditions, including SLE and multiple sclerosis in some populations
    HLA-DQ2 / DQ8Celiac disease

    Platelet refractoriness: Repeated transfusions can expose patients to HLA antigens, resulting in HLA alloimmunization and reduced platelet increments.

    12. Factors affecting immunogenicity

    Not every antigen produces the same immune response. Several factors influence immunogenicity.

    FactorExplanation
    ForeignnessThe more foreign a substance is, the more likely it is to be immunogenic
    Chemical compositionProteins are generally more immunogenic than polysaccharides, lipids and nucleic acids
    Molecular sizeLarger molecules are generally more immunogenic
    Molecular complexityComplex structures tend to stimulate stronger immune responses
    Susceptibility to processingAntigens must be processed and presented effectively
    Genetic compositionHLA and other inherited factors influence responses
    Route of administrationOral, intradermal, subcutaneous and intramuscular routes differ in immune stimulation
    DoseAn insufficient or excessively high dose may produce a poor response or tolerance
    Frequency of exposureRepeated exposures may increase the response
    AdjuvantsEnhance antigen presentation and immune activation

    Routes of antigen administration

    RouteAbbreviationAdministration
    OralPOThrough the mouth
    IntradermalIDInto the skin
    SubcutaneousSCBeneath the skin
    IntramuscularIMInto the muscle
    IntravenousIVInto a vein
    IntraperitonealIPInto the peritoneal cavity

    Adjuvants

    Adjuvants are added to vaccines to enhance immunogenicity.

    Examples:

    • Aluminum salts (alum).
    • Squalene-based adjuvants.
    • MF59.

    Functions:

    • Prolong antigen persistence.
    • Enhance antigen presentation.
    • Promote local inflammation.
    • Increase immune-cell activation.

    13. Antibodies / Immunoglobulins

    Antibodies are immunoglobulin proteins produced by plasma cells in response to antigenic stimulation.

    They are part of the humoral component of adaptive immunity.

    Structure of an antibody

    An antibody consists of:

    Two identical heavy chains.

    Two identical light chains.

    • Disulfide bonds connecting the chains.
    • Variable and constant regions.

    Antibody structural components

    ComponentFunction
    Variable regionDetermines antigen specificity
    Constant regionDetermines immunoglobulin class and effector function
    Fab regionAntigen-binding fragment
    Fc regionBinds Fc receptors and participates in complement activation
    Hinge regionProvides flexibility
    Disulfide bondsMaintain structural stability

    Light chains

    There are two types:

    • Kappa (κ)
    • Lambda (λ)

    An individual antibody contains either kappa or lambda light chains, not both within the same antibody molecule.

    Heavy chains and immunoglobulin classes

    Heavy chainImmunoglobulin
    Gamma (γ)IgG
    Alpha (α)IgA
    Mu (μ)IgM
    Epsilon (ε)IgE
    Delta (δ)IgD

    Papain versus pepsin digestion

    FeaturePapainPepsin
    Cleavage siteAbove hinge regionBelow hinge region
    ProductsTwo Fab fragments + one Fc fragmentOne F(ab')₂ fragment; Fc is degraded
    Antigen-binding abilityTwo separate binding fragmentsTwo binding sites remain connected
    AgglutinationFab fragments are generally unable to cross-link antigens effectivelyF(ab')₂ retains bivalent binding

    Memory aid:

    • Papain = 2 Fab + 1 Fc.
    • Pepsin = F(ab')₂.

    Five classes of immunoglobulins

    CharacteristicIgGIgMIgAIgEIgD
    Heavy chainγμαεδ
    Molecular structureMonomerPentamer in serum; monomer on B cellsMonomer in serum; dimer in secretionsMonomerMonomer
    Molecular weight (approx.)150 kDa900 kDa160 kDa monomer190 kDa180 kDa
    Percentage of serum Ig70–75%5–10%10–15%Trace0.2%
    Half-life21–23 days5 days5–6 days2 days2–3 days
    Placental transferYesNoNoNoNo
    Complement activationYes, especially IgG1 and IgG3StrongestGenerally noNoNo
    Main functionSecondary response, opsonization, neutralizationPrimary response, agglutinationMucosal immunityAllergy and parasitic defenseB-cell receptor

    Detailed functions of each immunoglobulin

    IgG

    • Most abundant immunoglobulin in serum.
    • Main antibody in the secondary immune response.
    • Crosses the placenta.
    • Opsonizes microorganisms.
    • Can activate complement depending on subclass.
    • Important in warm-reactive RBC antibodies.

    IgM

    • First antibody produced in the primary immune response.
    • Usually pentameric in circulation.
    • Most efficient immunoglobulin at agglutination.
    • Strong activator of the classical complement pathway.
    • Does not cross the placenta.
    • Often associated with cold-reactive antibodies.

    IgA

    • Main immunoglobulin in mucosal secretions.
    • Present in saliva, tears, breast milk and respiratory/GI secretions.
    • Secretory IgA is usually dimeric.
    • Has a secretory component that protects it from enzymatic degradation.

    IgE

    • Responsible for immediate-type hypersensitivity reactions.
    • Binds to mast cells and basophils.
    • Involved in parasitic immunity.
    • Mediates allergic responses.

    IgD

    • Primarily functions as a B-cell surface receptor.
    • Found alongside IgM on mature naïve B lymphocytes.
    • Present in very low serum concentrations.

    Primary versus secondary immune response

    CharacteristicPrimary responseSecondary response
    ExposureFirst encounterSubsequent encounter
    Lag phaseLongerShorter
    Main antibody initiallyIgMIgG, depending on antigen
    Antibody concentrationLowerHigher
    AffinityInitially lowerGenerally higher
    DurationShorterLonger
    Memory cellsGeneratedActivated rapidly

    EXAM TIP: Primary response = IgM first. Secondary response = rapid, stronger IgG response.

    IgG subclasses

    SubclassMain feature
    IgG1Most abundant; protein antigen response
    IgG2Important in response to polysaccharide antigens
    IgG3Strong complement activation
    IgG4Can undergo Fab-arm exchange; does not efficiently activate complement

    High-yield: IgG3 is particularly effective at activating complement among IgG subclasses.

    14. Complement system

    The complement system consists of plasma and membrane-associated proteins that enhance immune defense.

    It was discovered through the work of Jules Bordet.

    Complement proteins are generally designated using the letter C followed by a number.

    Examples:

    • C1 C2 C3 C4 C5

    Small cleavage fragments are generally designated with lowercase letters, such as C3a and C3b.

    Main functions of complement

    FunctionExplanationImportant components
    OpsonizationEnhances phagocytosisC3b
    InflammationPromotes inflammatory responsesC3a, C4a, C5a
    ChemotaxisAttracts leukocytesC5a
    Cell lysisDestroys target cells through MACC5b–C9
    Immune-complex clearanceHelps remove circulating immune complexesC3b and complement receptors

    Three pathways of complement activation

    All three pathways converge at C3 activation.

    FeatureClassical pathwayAlternative pathwayLectin pathway
    TriggerAntigen-antibody complexesMicrobial surfaces and spontaneous C3 activationMannose residues on microorganisms
    Main initiating componentC1 complexC3b, Factor B, Factor DMannose-binding lectin (MBL)
    Requires antibody?Usually yesNoNo
    C3 convertaseC4b2aC3bBbC4b2a
    C5 convertaseC4b2a3bC3bBbC3bC4b2a3b
    Final pathwayMACMACMAC

    Classical pathway

    Activated by antigen-antibody complexes, particularly involving IgM and IgG.

    Sequence:

    1. Antigen-antibody complex forms.
    2. C1q binds to the Fc portion of antibody.
    3. C1r and C1s become activated.
    1. C4 and C2 are cleaved.
    2. C4b2a forms the C3 convertase.
    3. C3 is cleaved.
    4. C5 convertase forms.
    5. MAC is assembled.

    Important: IgM is especially efficient because one antigen-bound pentamer can efficiently activate C1.

    Alternative pathway

    Does not require antibodies.

    Important proteins:

    • C3 Factor B Factor D Properdin

    Sequence:

    1. C3b binds a microbial surface.
    2. Factor B binds C3b.
    3. Factor D cleaves Factor B.
    4. C3bBb forms.
    5. Properdin stabilizes the C3 convertase.
    6. C3 activation continues.

    Lectin pathway

    Activated when mannose-binding lectin recognizes carbohydrate structures on microbial surfaces.

    Important proteins:

    • Mannose-binding lectin (MBL).
    • MASP-1.
    • MASP-2.

    The lectin pathway produces the same C3 convertase as the classical pathway.

    Important complement proteins

    C1rActivates C1s

    C3bOpsonization
    C4Classical and lectin pathways
    C4aAnaphylatoxin, relatively weak
    C5Cleaved to C5a and C5b
    C5aPowerful anaphylatoxin and chemotactic factor
    C5bInitiates MAC assembly
    C6Joins C5b in MAC
    C7Helps anchor MAC to membranes
    C8Contributes to membrane insertion
    C9Polymerizes to form MAC pores
    Factor BAlternative pathway C3 convertase formation
    Factor DCleaves Factor B
    ProperdinStabilizes alternative pathway C3 convertase
    MBLRecognizes microbial mannose
    MASP-1 / MASP-2Activate lectin pathway

    Complement regulatory proteins

    These prevent excessive complement activation and damage to normal host cells.

    Regulatory proteinFunction
    C1 inhibitor (C1-INH)Inhibits C1r and C1s and other proteases
    Factor HRegulates alternative pathway
    Factor ICleaves C3b and C4b with cofactors
    C4-binding proteinRegulates classical/lectin pathway
    CD55 (DAF)Accelerates decay of C3/C5 convertases
    CD59Prevents MAC formation
    MCP (CD46)Cofactor for Factor I-mediated cleavage

    Complement deficiencies and disease associations

    DeficiencyClinical association
    C1q, C2, C4Increased immune-complex disease and SLE-like manifestations
    C3Severe recurrent pyogenic infections; immune-complex disease
    C5–C9Recurrent Neisseria infections
    C1 inhibitorHereditary angioedema
    Factor H / Factor IIncreased alternative pathway activity and atypical HUS-related disease
    CD55 and CD59 deficiencyParoxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)

    High-yield clinical associations:

    • C3 deficiency → severe recurrent infections.
    • C5–C9 deficiency → recurrent Neisseria infections.
    • C1-INH deficiency → hereditary angioedema.
    • CD55/CD59 deficiency → PNH.

    TestWhat it measures
    CH50Functional integrity of the classical pathway and terminal pathway
    AH50Functional integrity of the alternative pathway and terminal pathway
    C3 concentrationQuantity of C3
    C4 concentrationQuantity of C4

    Interpretation:

    CH50AH50Possible interpretation
    LowNormalEarly classical pathway deficiency
    NormalLowAlternative pathway deficiency
    LowLowC3 or terminal pathway deficiency, or consumption
    NormalNormalNo major functional deficiency detected

    Remember: A low complement concentration may result from either reduced production or increased consumption.

    PART III. SEROLOGY

    15. Antigen-antibody interactions

    Serology studies antigen-antibody reactions and their application in the diagnosis of disease.

    Forces involved in antigen-antibody binding

    These interactions are generally noncovalent and reversible.

    ForceExplanation
    Hydrogen bondsAttraction between hydrogen-containing polar groups
    Electrostatic forcesAttraction between oppositely charged groups
    Van der Waals forcesWeak intermolecular attractions
    Hydrophobic interactionsAssociation of nonpolar regions away from water

    Important: Antigen-antibody binding is reversible, specific and dependent on the compatibility of the antigenic epitope and antibody paratope.

    Characteristics of antigen-antibody reactions

    1. Reversible – antibodies can dissociate from antigens.
    2. Specific – antibodies recognize particular epitopes.
    3. Sensitive – small amounts of antigen or antibody may be detected.
    4. Cross-reactive – an antibody may react with structurally similar epitopes on different antigens.

    Cross-reactivity

    Cross-reactivity occurs when an antibody reacts with an antigen other than the original immunizing antigen because of structural similarities.

    Example:

    - Antibodies generated against one microorganism may react with antigens from another microorganism with similar epitopes.

    Affinity versus avidity

    This distinction is frequently tested.

    AffinityAvidity
    Strength of binding between one antigenic epitope and one antibody-binding siteOverall binding strength of multivalent antigen- antibody interactions
    Individual interactionCombined interaction
    Describes one binding siteDescribes the entire complex
    Usually measured using binding constantsInfluenced by affinity and valency

    Memory aid: Affinity = individual grip; avidity = total grip.

    16. Agglutination and precipitation

    Agglutination

    Agglutination is the interaction of an antibody with a particulate antigen, resulting in visible clumping.

    Examples:

    • Blood typing.
    • Widal test.
    • Weil-Felix test.
    • Latex agglutination.
    • Bacterial agglutination.

    Precipitation

    Precipitation occurs when an antibody reacts with a soluble antigen, producing an insoluble antigen-antibody lattice.

    Examples:

    • Immunodiffusion.
    • Immunoelectrophoresis.
    • Nephelometry-based immune-complex measurement.

    Agglutination versus precipitation

    FeatureAgglutinationPrecipitation
    AntigenParticulateSoluble
    Reaction productVisible clumpingInsoluble precipitate
    Antigen examplesRBCs, bacteria, latex particlesSoluble proteins
    Typical applicationBlood grouping, microbial serologyProtein identification and immunodiffusion
    Visual resultAgglutinated particlesPrecipitin line or precipitate

    Stages of agglutination

    Stage 1: Sensitization / coating

    Antibody binds to antigen on the surface of a particle.

    No visible clumping is necessarily present.

    Stage 2: Lattice formation

    Antibodies cross-link antigen-bearing particles, forming aggregates that can be seen macroscopically.

    Types of agglutination

    TypePrincipleExamples
    Direct agglutinationNaturally occurring particulate antigen reacts with antibodyWidal, Weil-Felix, RBC typing
    Passive agglutinationSoluble antigen is attached artificially to a carrier particleTP-PA, latex antigen tests
    Reverse passive agglutinationAntibody is attached to carrier particles to detect antigenCertain bacterial antigen detection tests
    Agglutination inhibitionSoluble antigen inhibits visible agglutinationPregnancy testing
    HemagglutinationRBCs act as particlesABO typing
    Hemagglutination inhibitionInhibition of RBC agglutination by specific antibodiesViral antibody testing

    Direct agglutination

    The antigen is naturally present on the particle.

    Examples:

    • Widal test.
    • Weil-Felix test.
    • Forward ABO typing.
    • Rh typing.
    • Bacterial agglutination.

    Passive agglutination

    Soluble antigen is artificially attached to a carrier, such as latex particles.

    Examples:

    • Latex agglutination for certain microbial antigens.
    • TP-PA (Treponema pallidum particle agglutination).

    Reverse passive agglutination

    Antibodies are attached to particles to detect soluble antigen.

    Agglutination inhibition

    This is a particularly important concept.

    The presence of the analyte prevents the expected visible agglutination.

    Pregnancy test principle:

    In a classical agglutination-inhibition pregnancy test:

    • hCG in the patient's urine reacts with anti-hCG.
    • This prevents the anti-hCG from binding to hCG-coated particles.
    • No agglutination = positive for hCG.
    • Agglutination = negative for hCG.

    Modern pregnancy tests are generally lateral-flow immunochromatographic assays, but the classical inhibition principle remains important for examinations.

    17. Prozone and postzone phenomena

    Antigen-antibody reactions depend on the correct proportion of antigen and antibody.

    Zone of equivalence

    The ideal proportion of antigen and antibody where extensive lattice formation occurs.

    ZoneConditionEffectSolution
    ProzoneAntibody excessFalse-negative or weak reactionDilute patient serum
    EquivalenceOptimal antigen- antibody ratioStrongest reactionNo correction necessary
    PostzoneAntigen excessFalse-negative or weak reactionDilute antigen-containing specimen or use an appropriate method

    EXAM TIP:

    • Prozone = too much antibody.
    • Postzone = too much antigen.
    • Equivalence = ideal ratio.

    Why do these cause false negatives?

    Lattice formation requires sufficient antigen and antibody cross-linking.

    If there is too much of one reactant, optimal cross-linking is impaired.

    18. Antigen-antibody reaction factors

    FactorImportant concept
    Antigen-antibody ratioZone of equivalence produces optimal reactions
    pHOptimal pH is generally around 6.5–7.5
    TemperatureInfluences reaction rate and antibody reactivity
    CentrifugationBrings antigen and antibody into closer contact
    Ionic strengthReduced ionic strength enhances some antibody-antigen interactions
    Incubation timeAllows sufficient binding
    Antigen densityMore accessible antigen sites can enhance reactions
    Antibody classIgM generally agglutinates more effectively than IgG
    Zeta potentialInfluences the distance between RBCs

    Important blood banking reaction enhancers

    Low ionic strength solution (LISS)

    • Reduces ionic strength of the medium.
    • Accelerates antibody uptake by RBCs.
    • Reduces incubation time.

    Polyethylene glycol (PEG)

    • Enhances antibody detection by reducing available free water.
    • Concentrates antibody molecules near RBC antigens.
    • Commonly used for detecting weak antibodies.

    Albumin

    • Reduces zeta potential.
    • Facilitates RBC agglutination.
    • Can enhance some antibody reactions.

    Zeta potential

    RBCs normally possess a negative surface charge due largely to sialic acid.

    This produces repulsion between RBCs, preventing them from coming into close contact.

    MethodEffect on zeta potential / reaction
    AlbuminReduces repulsive forces
    Enzyme treatmentRemoves some negatively charged surface components
    LISSEnhances antibody uptake; does not simply remove zeta potential
    PEGEnhances antibody detection through concentration effects

    Temperature and antibody class

    TemperatureCommon antibody typeExamples
    4°CCold-reactiveAnti-M, anti-N, anti-P1, Lewis antibodies
    Room temperatureOften cold-reactiveSome IgM antibodies
    30–37°CWarm-reactiveMost clinically significant IgG antibodies
    37°C/AHGClinically significant warm antibodiesRh, Kell, Duffy, Kidd

    Important: Temperature association is not absolute. Clinical significance depends on thermal amplitude, immunoglobulin class, complement activation and transfusion relevance.

    19. Antigen-antibody detection methods

    Serologic testing detects and measures antigens or antibodies.

    Major forms of serologic tests

    Test typePrincipleExample
    AgglutinationVisible clumpingABO typing
    PrecipitationFormation of insoluble immune complexesImmunodiffusion
    Labeled immunoassayUses labeled antigen or antibodyELISA
    Complement-related testMeasures complement fixation or activityComplement fixation test
    Neutralization / inhibitionAntibody inhibits a biological activityASO-related inhibition
    Nucleic acid testDetects genetic materialPCR

    Qualitative, quantitative and semiquantitative tests

    TypeResult
    QualitativePositive or negative
    QuantitativeNumerical concentration
    SemiquantitativeTiter or approximate concentration

    20. Titer and dilution calculations

    Titer is the reciprocal of the highest dilution of a specimen that still produces a positive reaction.

    Example:

    If a specimen remains positive up to 1:160 but becomes negative at 1:320:

    Titer = 160.

    Serial dilution

    In serial dilution, each subsequent tube is diluted using a fixed dilution factor.

    Example of twofold serial dilution:

    TubeDilution
    11:20
    21:40
    31:80
    41:160
    51:320
    61:640

    The titer is the reciprocal of the last positive dilution.

    Interpreting agglutination results

    TubeResult
    1:20Positive
    1:40Positive
    1:80Positive
    1:160Positive
    1:320Negative
    1:640Negative

    Titer = 160.

    Dilution formula

    Volume of sample
    Dilution =
    Total volume

    For example, mixing 5 mL of sample with 15 mL of diluent:

    5
    1
    =
    5 + 15
    4

    Therefore, the dilution is 1:4.

    Determining the amount of diluent

    To prepare a 1:20 dilution using 5 mL of sample:

    Total volume = 5(20) = 100 mL
    Diluent = 100 −5 = 95 mL

    Serial dilution shortcut

    For serial dilutions, multiply the dilution factors.

    Example:

    A 1:2 dilution followed by a 1:4 dilution:

    2 × 4 = 8

    Final dilution = 1:8.

    21. Precipitation techniques

    Precipitation is an antigen-antibody reaction involving soluble antigens.

    Measurement techniques

    MethodPrincipleDetection
    NephelometryMeasures scattered lightIncreased scattered light
    TurbidimetryMeasures reduction in transmitted lightIncreased turbidity
    ImmunodiffusionAntigen and antibody diffuse through gelPrecipitin line
    ImmunoelectrophoresisElectrophoresis followed by immunodiffusionPrecipitin arcs

    Remember:

    • Nephelometry = scattered light.
    • Turbidimetry = reduced transmitted light.

    Passive immunodiffusion

    MethodPrinciple
    Single radial immunodiffusion (SRID)Antigen diffuses radially into antibody-containing gel
    Single linear immunodiffusionAntigen diffuses in one direction
    Double immunodiffusion (Ouchterlony)Antigen and antibody diffuse toward each other
    Kinetic immunodiffusionMeasures reaction over time

    Electrophoresis

    Electrophoresis separates molecules based on their movement in an electric field.

    TechniqueMain application
    Zone electrophoresisSeparation of serum proteins
    ImmunoelectrophoresisIdentification of immunoglobulins
    Immunofixation electrophoresisIdentification of monoclonal immunoglobulins
    Crossed immunoelectrophoresisSeparation followed by antigen-antibody precipitation

    Serum protein electrophoresis

    The major fractions are:

    1. Albumin.
    2. Alpha-1 globulin.
    1. Alpha-2 globulin.
    2. Beta globulin.
    3. Gamma globulin.

    Important: Albumin is the largest fraction in normal serum. The gamma region contains most immunoglobulins.

    Immunofixation electrophoresis

    Used to identify monoclonal immunoglobulins.

    Procedure:

    1. Serum proteins are separated by electrophoresis.
    2. Antisera against heavy and light chains are applied.
    3. Antigen-antibody complexes form.
    4. The pattern identifies the immunoglobulin type.

    Clinical association: Multiple myeloma and other monoclonal gammopathies.

    22. Labeled immunoassays

    These tests use a labeled antigen or antibody to detect an immune reaction.

    Types of labels

    LabelDetection method
    EnzymeSpectrophotometry / color change
    FluorochromeFluorescence microscopy or fluorometry
    RadioisotopeRadiation measurement
    Chemiluminescent labelLight emission

    ELISA / EIA

    Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay detects antigens or antibodies using enzyme-labeled reagents.

    Types of ELISA

    TypeWhat is detected?Principle

    Indirect ELISAAntibodyPatient antibody binds antigen; enzyme-labeled secondary antibody detects it
    Sandwich ELISAAntigenAntigen is captured between two antibodies

    23. Complement fixation test (CFT)

    The complement fixation test detects antibodies capable of fixing complement.

    Principle

    The test uses an antigen-antibody reaction to determine whether complement is consumed.

    Important: In the classical complement fixation test, NO HEMOLYSIS means a positive

    result.

    Procedure

    1. Patient serum is heated to inactivate endogenous complement.
    2. Known antigen is added.
    3. A measured amount of complement is added.
    4. The mixture is incubated.
    5. Sensitized sheep RBCs are added.
    6. Hemolysis is observed.

    Interpretation

    ResultInterpretation
    No hemolysisPositive – complement was fixed by antigen-antibody complexes
    HemolysisNegative – complement remained available to lyse sensitized RBCs

    Memory aid: CFT = complement consumed = no hemolysis = positive.

    24. Neutralization / inhibition tests

    These tests determine whether antibodies can neutralize the biological activity of an antigen or toxin.

    Antistreptolysin O (ASO) test

    The ASO test detects antibodies against streptolysin O, a toxin produced by Group A Streptococcus.

    Clinical relevance:

    • Recent streptococcal infection.
    • Acute rheumatic fever.
    • Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

    Pathophysiology

    Group A Streptococcus can produce streptolysin O, which is oxygen-labile and hemolytic.

    The patient develops antibodies against streptolysin O.

    When patient serum contains ASO:

    • The antibodies neutralize streptolysin O.
    • Hemolysis is inhibited.

    ASO interpretation

    FindingInterpretation
    Increased ASO titerEvidence supporting recent streptococcal infection
    Normal ASODoes not completely exclude infection
    Rising paired titersStronger evidence of recent infection

    The source gives a conventional reference value of less than 200 Todd units. Actual reference limits depend on age, population and laboratory method.

    Diseases following Group A Streptococcus infection

    DiseaseMechanism
    Acute rheumatic feverAutoimmune cross-reactivity following streptococcal infection
    Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritisImmune-complex-related renal injury

    Strand-displacement amplificationAmplifies nucleic acid through strand displacement
