    PART IV. BLOOD BANKING AND TRANSFUSION MEDICINE

    26. Fundamentals of blood banking

    Blood banking involves the collection, processing, testing, storage and distribution of blood and blood components for transfusion.

    Transfusion medicine involves the clinical use of blood and blood components.

    Why is blood banking important?

    Blood contains:

    • RBC antigens.
    • Plasma antibodies.
    • Other cellular and soluble components.

    An antigen-antibody reaction between incompatible donor and recipient blood can cause RBC destruction.

    Historical figures

    PersonContribution
    Pope Innocent VIIIAssociated with an early historical attempted transfusion
    James BlundellEarly successful human-to-human blood transfusion
    Karl LandsteinerDiscovery of the ABO blood group system, 1901
    Jan JanskýClassification of blood into four groups
    Alexander WienerImportant contributions to Rh blood group research

    Immunologic and serologic principles

    In blood banking:

    • Antigens are present on RBCs.
    • Antibodies are present in plasma or serum.
    • Antigen-antibody reactions may result in agglutination or hemolysis.
    • Compatibility testing identifies potentially harmful interactions.

    Golden rule:

    Never allow the antigen of one individual to meet the corresponding antibody of another incompatible individual.

    27. Naturally occurring versus immune antibodies

    This is one of the most important blood banking comparisons.

    FeatureNaturally occurring antibodiesImmune antibodies
    FormationDevelop without known intentional immunizationDevelop following exposure to foreign RBC antigens
    Exposure requiredNot necessarilyYes
    Common immunoglobulinUsually IgMUsually IgG
    TemperatureOften cold-reactiveOften warm-reactive
    ExamplesAnti-A, anti-B, anti-A,B; some Lewis and MNS antibodiesAnti-D, anti-K, anti-c, anti-Jka
    Complement activationSome activate complement stronglyDepends on antibody
    Clinical significanceVariableFrequently clinically significant

    Naturally occurring antibodies

    The ABO system is the classic example.

    A person generally develops antibodies against ABO antigens they lack.

    Immune antibodies

    These form after exposure through:

    1. Blood transfusion.
    1. Pregnancy.
    2. Transplantation.

    Examples:

    • Anti-D.
    • Anti-K.
    • Anti-E.
    • Anti-Jka.

    ABO antibodies

    Blood groupRBC antigenPlasma antibody
    AAAnti-B
    BBAnti-A
    ABA and BNone
    ONeither A nor BAnti-A and anti-B

    Rh antibodies

    Rh statusAnti-D
    D-positiveUsually absent unless immunized
    D-negativeMay develop following exposure to D-positive RBCs

    Important: Rh antibodies are not naturally occurring in the same way as ABO antibodies. Anti-D generally develops following exposure.

    28. Cold-reactive versus warm-reactive antibodies

    FeatureCold-reactiveWarm-reactive
    Optimal temperature4°C or colder37°C
    Common immunoglobulinIgMIgG
    ReactivityImmediate-spin / saline phase37°C and AHG phase
    Clinical significanceUsually insignificant, depending on thermal amplitudeOften clinically significant
    ExamplesAnti-M, anti-N, anti-P1, anti-Lea, anti-LebAnti-D, anti-C, anti-E, anti-K, anti- Fya, anti-Jka
    HemolysisMay cause complement-mediated intravascular hemolysisUsually extravascular hemolysis

    Clinical significance

    A cold-reactive antibody is generally more concerning when it reacts at temperatures closer to 30–37°C.

    Thermal amplitude is more clinically important than simply observing a reaction at 4°C.

    Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (WAIHA)

    • Usually associated with IgG.
    • Often reacts optimally at 37°C.
    • May produce extravascular hemolysis.
    • Commonly associated with the Rh blood group system.

    Cold autoimmune hemolytic conditions

    ConditionImportant antibody
    Cold agglutinin diseaseOften anti-I
    Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuriaUsually anti-P, a biphasic IgG antibody

    Donath-Landsteiner test: Used to detect the biphasic hemolysin associated with paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria.

    29. Alloantibodies versus autoantibodies

    AlloantibodiesAutoantibodies
    Directed against antigens from another individual of the same speciesDirected against the individual's own antigens
    Develop following exposure to foreign antigensDevelop due to loss of self-tolerance
    May be detected during antibody screeningMay produce a positive autocontrol
    Example: anti-D after transfusion or pregnancyExample: warm autoanti-IgG

    Clinical distinction:

    • Alloantibody → donor antigen incompatibility.
    • Autoantibody → reacts with the patient's own RBCs.

    30. Monoclonal versus polyclonal antibodies

    FeatureMonoclonalPolyclonal
    OriginOne B-cell cloneMultiple B-cell clones
    Antigen recognitionOne specific epitopeMultiple epitopes
    CompositionHomogeneousHeterogeneous
    SpecificityHighly specificBroader
    ProductionHybridoma technology or recombinant methodsImmunization of animals or natural immune responses
    ApplicationDiagnostic reagents, targeted therapiesGeneral immunologic detection and research

    Hybridoma technology

    Developed through the work of Georges Köhler and César Milstein.

    The technique involves:

    1. Immunizing an animal with an antigen.
    2. Isolating antibody-producing B lymphocytes.
    3. Fusing B cells with immortal myeloma cells.
    4. Selecting hybridoma cells.
    5. Cloning and expanding the desired antibody-producing hybridoma.

    High-yield: Hybridoma technology produces monoclonal antibodies.

    PART V. ABO BLOOD GROUP SYSTEM

    31. ABO blood group system

    The ABO system is the most important blood group system in routine transfusion practice.

    It was discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1901.

    ABO incompatibility can cause severe, potentially fatal acute hemolytic transfusion reactions.

    ABO blood group table

    Blood typeRBC antigenPlasma antibodyGenotype
    AAAnti-BAA or AO
    BBAnti-ABB or BO
    ABA and BNoneAB
    ONoneAnti-A and anti-BOO

    ABO inheritance

    The ABO gene is located on chromosome 9.

    The alleles are:

    • A B O

    A and B are codominant.

    O is recessive.

    Mendelian laws relevant to ABO

    LawMeaning
    Law of segregationAlleles separate during gamete formation
    Law of independent assortmentGenes for separate traits are inherited independently when not linked
    Law of dominanceA dominant allele can mask a recessive allele

    Homozygous versus heterozygous

    TermMeaningExample
    HomozygousTwo identical allelesAA, BB, OO
    HeterozygousTwo different allelesAO, BO

    Possible ABO inheritance

    ParentsPossible offspring
    O × OO
    A × OA or O
    B × OB or O
    AB × OA or B
    A × BA, B, AB or O (if both are heterozygous)
    AB × ABA, B or AB
    A × AA or O (if both are AO)
    B × BB or O (if both are BO)

    Important terminology

    Dosage effect: Homozygous expression of an antigen may produce stronger reactions than heterozygous expression.

    Example:

    • AA may express more A antigen than AO.
    • Some antibodies react more strongly with homozygous antigen-positive cells.

    Codominance: Both alleles are expressed simultaneously.

    Example: AB blood group.

    Amorph / silent gene: An allele that produces no detectable antigen or phenotypic product under the relevant conditions.

    32. Biochemistry of ABO antigens

    ABO antigens are carbohydrate structures found on RBC membranes and other tissues.

    They are synthesized through the action of glycosyltransferase enzymes.

    Development of ABO antigens

    ABO antigens develop during fetal life, but their expression is not fully mature at birth.

    The source identifies approximately the 37th day of fetal life as the early development point.

    H substance

    The H antigen is the precursor substance needed for the formation of A and B antigens.

    The FUT1 gene encodes an α-1,2-fucosyltransferase responsible for forming H antigen on RBCs.

    ABO antigen synthesis

    Blood groupEnzymeSugar addedFinal antigen
    ONo functional A or B transferaseNo additional A/B sugarH remains unchanged
    AA transferaseN-acetylgalactosamineA antigen
    BB transferaseGalactoseB antigen
    ABBoth transferasesBoth sugarsA and B antigens

    Important:

    • A antigen → N-acetylgalactosamine.
    • B antigen → D-galactose.
    • H antigen → L-fucose.

    H antigen expression

    The H antigen is generally most abundant on group O RBCs because it is not converted into A or B antigen.

    The amount of H antigen generally follows:

    O > A
    >
    B > A
    B >
    >
    A
    A
    B

    2

    2

    1

    1

    The exact expression depends on the phenotype and underlying genotype.

    ABO antibodies

    CharacteristicABO antibodies
    DevelopmentUsually develop during the first months of life
    Main immunoglobulinIgM
    Other classIgG may occur, especially in group O
    ReactivityUsually room temperature or colder
    ComplementCan activate classical complement pathway
    Clinical significanceMajor cause of acute hemolytic transfusion reactions

    High-yield: Group O individuals may possess both IgM and clinically significant IgG anti-A and anti-B.

    33. ABO blood typing

    ABO typing consists of two complementary procedures:

    1. Forward typing.
    2. Reverse typing.

    Forward versus reverse typing

    FeatureForward typingReverse typing
    Other nameCell typingSerum typing
    SpecimenPatient RBCsPatient serum/plasma
    DetectsA and B antigensAnti-A and anti-B antibodies
    ReagentsAnti-A, anti-BA1 cells, B cells
    Positive reactionAgglutinationAgglutination
    PurposeIdentifies RBC antigensConfirms ABO group

    Forward typing interpretation

    Blood groupAnti-AAnti-B
    A+−
    B−+
    AB++
    O−−

    Reverse typing interpretation

    Blood groupA1 cellsB cells
    A−+
    B+−
    AB−−
    O++

    Remember: Forward typing detects the antigen; reverse typing detects the antibody.

    ABO discrepancy

    An ABO discrepancy occurs when forward and reverse typing results do not agree.

    Four major types of ABO discrepancy

    TypeCauseExamples
    Type IWeak or missing antibodiesNewborns, elderly patients, immunodeficiency, immunosuppressive therapy
    Type IIWeak or missing antigensA or B subgroups, leukemia, hematologic malignancy
    Type IIIPlasma or protein abnormalitiesRouleaux, elevated globulins, fibrinogen, plasma expanders
    Type IVMiscellaneous causesCold-reactive antibodies, unexpected alloantibodies, technical errors

    Resolution of ABO discrepancies

    • Repeat testing and verify patient identity.
    • Check reagent and specimen integrity.
    • Review patient history.
    • Perform appropriate cell washing.
    • Consider incubation at room temperature or colder when indicated.
    • Investigate rouleaux.
    • Perform additional testing for weak subgroups.
    • Use specialized testing if Bombay phenotype is suspected.

    Important: Never assign an ABO group until the discrepancy is satisfactorily resolved.

    34. Bombay phenotype

    The Bombay phenotype is a rare blood group phenotype characterized by the absence of H antigen on RBCs.

    It is usually associated with the hh genotype.

    Characteristics

    FeatureBombay phenotype
    H antigenAbsent
    A antigenCannot be expressed normally
    B antigenCannot be expressed normally
    Anti-HPresent
    Anti-AMay be present
    Anti-BMay be present
    Anti-A,BMay be present
    Reaction with anti-H lectinNo agglutination
    CompatibilityRequires Bombay-compatible blood

    Bombay versus ordinary group O

    TestOrdinary OBombay (Oh)
    Anti-ANo agglutinationNo agglutination
    Anti-BNo agglutinationNo agglutination
    Anti-H lectinStrong agglutinationNo agglutination
    Serum against O cellsUsually compatibleMay agglutinate
    H antigenPresentAbsent

    Most important distinction: Both may appear group O in routine forward typing, but Bombay individuals have anti-H and cannot receive ordinary group O RBCs.

    35. Secretor system

    The secretor gene is designated Se and is associated with the FUT2 gene.

    It determines whether ABO-related substances are present in body secretions.

    Examples:

    • Saliva.
    • Tears.
    • Urine.
    • Gastric secretions.
    • Semen.
    • Breast milk.

    Secretor versus nonsecretor

    FeatureSecretorNonsecretor
    GenotypeSeSe or Sesesese
    ABO substances in secretionsPresentAbsent or not detectable
    H substance in secretionsPresentAbsent
    Clinical significanceForensic and microbiologic associationsSome disease-susceptibility associations

    Important distinction: FUT1 is primarily responsible for H antigen expression on RBCs, while FUT2 is associated with secretor status in secretions.

    36. Lewis blood group system

    The Lewis system is unusual because its antigens are produced in tissues and adsorbed onto RBC membranes from plasma.

    The major antigens are:

    • Leᵃ Leᵇ

    Lewis phenotype

    PhenotypeGenotype patternAntigen expression
    Le(a+b−)Le present; Se absentLea
    Le(a−b+)Le present; Se presentLeb
    Le(a−b−)Le absentNeither
    Le(a+b+)Uncommon / transitionalBoth may be detectable

    Lewis characteristics

    • Lewis antigens are not primarily synthesized by RBCs.
    • They are adsorbed onto the RBC membrane.
    • Antigens may be present in body fluids.
    • Antibodies are usually naturally occurring IgM.
    • They are commonly cold-reactive.
    • They are generally not clinically significant.

    EXAM TIP: Lewis antibodies are usually neutralized by soluble Lewis substances in plasma or secretions.

    PART VI. RH BLOOD GROUP SYSTEM

    37. Rh blood group system

    The Rh system is one of the most clinically significant blood group systems.

    The most important antigen is D.

    Rh nomenclature

    SystemExample
    Fisher-RaceC, c, D, E, e
    WienerR⁰, R¹, R², Rᶻ, r, etc.
    RosenfieldNumeric antigen terminology
    ISBTStandardized numeric terminology

    Fisher-Race versus Wiener nomenclature

    Fisher-RaceWienerCommon meaning
    DceR⁰D+C? No; D, c, e expressed
    DCeR¹D, C, e
    DcER²D, c, E
    DCERᶻD, C, E
    dcerNo D, c, e
    dCer′No D, C, e
    dcEr″No D, c, E
    dCErʸNo D, C, E

    Note: The lowercase d is a conventional symbol indicating absence of D; it is not a true Rh antigen.

    Rh antigen characteristics

    • Rh antigens are protein antigens.
    • The major Rh genes are located on chromosome 1.
    • Rh antigens are generally well developed at birth.
    • D is highly immunogenic.
    • Rh antibodies are usually immune IgG antibodies.
    • Rh antibodies can cross the placenta.
    • They can cause hemolytic transfusion reactions and HDFN.

    Rh antigens

    AntigenImportance
    DMost immunogenic Rh antigen
    CClinically significant
    cClinically significant
    EClinically significant
    eClinically significant

    Rh antibodies

    CharacteristicRh antibodies
    FormationUsually following transfusion or pregnancy
    ImmunoglobulinPredominantly IgG
    ReactivityWarm-reactive
    ComplementUsually do not efficiently activate complement
    Clinical significanceFrequently significant
    Disease associationHDFN and delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions

    38. Rh typing

    Rh typing determines whether the patient's RBCs express the D antigen.

    Principle

    Patient RBCs are mixed with anti-D reagent.

    ResultInterpretation
    AgglutinationD-positive
    No agglutinationD-negative or possible weak D

    Weak D

    Weak D is characterized by reduced expression of the D antigen.

    Causes include:

    • Genetic weak D.
    • Partial D.
    • Position effect.
    • Other variations in RHD expression.

    Weak D testing

    Principle: Indirect antiglobulin test (IAT).

    Procedure

    1. Mix patient RBCs with anti-D.
    2. Incubate at 37°C according to reagent instructions.
    3. Wash the cells at least three times.
    4. Add antihuman globulin (AHG).
    5. Centrifuge and observe for agglutination.

    Interpretation

    ResultInterpretation
    Agglutination after AHGWeak D detected
    No agglutination after AHGWeak D not detected

    Why wash three times?

    To remove unbound anti-D antibodies. Residual free antibodies can neutralize the AHG reagent and cause false-negative results.

    Important clinical update: Molecular RHD genotyping is preferred for resolving certain weak D variants. Individuals with weak D types 1, 2 or 3 can generally be managed as D-positive, while other variants may require D-negative management.

    39. Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN)

    HDFN occurs when maternal antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal RBCs.

    Pathophysiology

    1. D-negative mother is exposed to D-positive fetal RBCs.
    2. Maternal immune system recognizes D antigen as foreign.
    3. Mother produces anti-D IgG.
    4. In a subsequent pregnancy, maternal IgG crosses the placenta.
    5. Antibodies bind fetal RBCs.
    6. Fetal RBC destruction causes anemia and may lead to hydrops fetalis.

    General requirements

    RequirementSignificance
    Mother lacks the relevant antigenCan form an antibody
    Fetus possesses the antigenTarget for maternal antibody
    Maternal antibody is IgGCan cross the placenta
    Antibody is clinically significantCan cause RBC destruction

    Rh immune globulin (RhIG / RhoGAM)

    RhIG is administered to prevent Rh-negative mothers from becoming sensitized to D- positive fetal RBCs.

    Mechanism: It promotes clearance of fetal D-positive RBCs from maternal circulation before the maternal immune system develops its own anti-D response.

    Administration

    The source identifies:

    • Routine prophylaxis at approximately 28 weeks of gestation.
    • Administration within 72 hours after delivery of a D-positive infant.
    • Additional administration after potentially sensitizing events.

    Important: The dose depends on the amount of fetomaternal hemorrhage and the specific product/protocol.

    Who is eligible?

    Generally:

    • D-negative mother.
    • No existing immune anti-D.
    • D-positive or potentially D-positive fetus.

    RhIG is not useful for a mother who has already developed immune anti-D.

    Fetomaternal hemorrhage (FMH)

    FMH refers to the passage of fetal RBCs into maternal circulation.

    Tests for FMH

    TestPrinciple
    Rosette testQualitative screening for fetal D-positive RBCs in D-negative maternal blood
    Kleihauer-Betke testDetects HbF-containing fetal RBCs through acid elution
    Flow cytometryQuantifies fetal RBCs using specific markers

    RhIG calculation

    The source includes these calculations:

    1. Percentage of fetal cells

    Fetal cells counted
    ×
    %Fetal cells =
    100
    Total RBCs counted

    2. Estimated FMH volume

    % fetal cells
    FMH =
    ×
    Maternal blood volume
    100

    3. Number of RhIG vials

    The source uses:

    FMH in mL
    Number of vials =
    30

    For whole blood, a 30 mL fetal whole-blood coverage assumption is used per standard 300 µg dose. For packed RBC volume, the corresponding assumption is approximately 15 mL.

    Rounding rule in the reviewer: Round to the nearest whole number, then add one vial according to the stated calculation protocol. Actual laboratory policy and product labeling should govern clinical dosing.

    40. Antibody screening

    Antibody screening detects unexpected clinically significant RBC antibodies in donor or recipient serum/plasma.

    Purpose

    • Detect unexpected antibodies.
    • Prevent hemolytic transfusion reactions.
    • Identify antibodies before transfusion.
    • Determine the need for antigen-negative donor RBCs.

    Major blood group systems screened

    Blood group systemImportant antigens
    RhD, C, c, E, e
    KellK, k
    KiddJka, Jkb
    DuffyFya, Fyb
    MNSM, N, S, s
    LewisLea, Leb
    PP1

    Antibody screening procedure

    The source describes a three-phase method.

    PhaseProcedurePurpose
    1. Immediate spinPatient serum + screening cells; centrifugeDetects mainly ABO-related and some cold- reactive antibodies
    2. 37°C phaseIncubate with LISSPromotes IgG sensitization
    3. AHG phaseWash cells, add AHG, centrifugeDetects IgG antibodies attached to RBCs

    Reagents

    ReagentPurpose
    Screening cellsKnown RBC antigen profiles
    LISSEnhances antibody uptake
    AHGDetects RBC-bound human immunoglobulin and/or complement
    SalineWashing and suspension medium
    Check cellsValidate negative AHG reactions

    Grading agglutination reactions

    GradeAppearance
    0No agglutination or hemolysis
    W+Tiny agglutinates; turbid background
    1+Small agglutinates; turbid background
    2+Medium-sized agglutinates; clear background
    3+Several large agglutinates; clear background
    4+One solid agglutinate

    Important: The source's exact grading descriptions should be used when answering questions based on its grading chart.

    Antibody screen interpretation

    ResultNext step
    PositivePerform antibody identification
    NegativeProceed to compatibility testing / crossmatching according to protocol

    41. Antibody identification

    Antibody identification is performed following a positive antibody screen.

    It determines which RBC antigen is being targeted by the patient's antibody.

    Procedure

    1. Test patient serum against an identification panel.
    2. Identify which panel cells react.
    3. Compare positive and negative reaction patterns.
    4. Review antigen profiles of panel cells.
    5. Apply rule-outs.
    6. Identify possible antibody specificity.
    7. Confirm using selected cells and additional techniques.

    Important rules in antibody identification

    Rule of three:

    To establish an antibody specificity, a common conventional approach requires:

    • Three antigen-positive cells reacting.
    • Three antigen-negative cells not reacting.

    This is a statistical confidence convention, not a substitute for evaluating all clinically relevant findings.

    Autocontrol

    ResultInterpretation
    Positive autocontrolPossible autoantibody or antibody coating the patient's RBCs
    Negative autocontrolMore consistent with alloantibody, although not definitive

    DAT versus IAT

    FeatureDATIAT
    Full nameDirect antiglobulin testIndirect antiglobulin test
    DetectsIn vivo sensitizationIn vitro sensitization
    SpecimenPatient RBCsPatient serum/plasma and test RBCs
    PrincipleDetects IgG and/or complement already bound to RBCsDetects antibodies that bind RBC antigens during incubation
    Common applicationsAIHA, HDFN, transfusion reactionsAntibody screening, identification, AHG crossmatch

    Remember:

    • DAT = antibody already attached inside the body.
    • IAT = antibody sensitization performed in the laboratory.

    42. Additional antibody identification techniques

    Enzyme treatment

    Enzymes modify RBC membrane structures and can enhance or destroy certain blood group antigens.

    EnzymeAntigens commonly enhancedAntigens commonly destroyed or weakened
    PapainRh, Kidd, Lewis, P1Duffy, M, N, some MNS antigens
    FicinSimilar to papainSimilar to papain
    BromelinRh, Kidd, LewisDuffy and some MNS antigens
    TrypsinSome Rh and Kidd reactionsDuffy and certain MNS antigens

    Important enzyme rule:

    • Rh, Kidd, Lewis and P1 → often enhanced.
    • Duffy, M and N → commonly destroyed or weakened.

    Why are enzymes used?

    Enzyme treatment can:

    • Increase antigen accessibility.
    • Enhance weak antibody reactions.
    • Help differentiate antibody specificities.

    Caution: Enzyme enhancement alone does not establish antibody specificity.

    Neutralization / inhibition

    Certain soluble substances can neutralize antibodies and help identify their specificity.

    SubstanceAntibody neutralized
    Hydatid cyst fluid, pigeon droppings, turtle-dove egg whiteAnti-P1
    Plasma or serumAnti-Lea and anti-Leb
    UrineAnti-Sda
    Human breast milkAnti-I

    Direct antiglobulin test (DAT)

    Detects in vivo sensitization of RBCs by IgG and/or complement.

    Clinical applications:

    • Autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
    • Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.
    • Hemolytic transfusion reactions.

    Elution

    Elution removes antibodies from sensitized RBCs.

    The antibody-containing eluate can then be tested to identify antibody specificity.

    Adsorption

    Adsorption removes antibodies from serum by allowing them to bind to RBC antigens.

    Applications:

    • Separation of alloantibodies from autoantibodies.
    • Investigation of complex antibody mixtures.

    Sulfhydryl reagents

    Examples:

    • 2-mercaptoethanol (2-ME).
    • Dithiothreitol (DTT).

    These break disulfide bonds and can destroy IgM antibody activity while generally preserving IgG activity.

    High-yield: DTT treatment can destroy Kell antigens. Therefore, anti-K detection may be affected when DTT-treated RBCs are used.

    43. Crossmatching

    Crossmatching is the final serologic compatibility test performed before RBC transfusion.

    Purpose

    To identify unexpected incompatibility between donor RBCs and recipient plasma.

    Types of crossmatch

    TypeComponentsWhat it detects
    Major crossmatchDonor RBCs + recipient serum/plasmaAntibodies in recipient against donor RBCs
    Minor crossmatchDonor serum/plasma + recipient RBCsAntibodies in donor plasma against recipient RBCs
    AutocontrolPatient RBCs + patient serumAutoantibodies or self-reactivity

    Major crossmatch is the clinically important routine compatibility test.

    Crossmatch phases

    PhaseTemperature / reagentPurpose
    Immediate spinRoom temperatureDetects ABO incompatibility
    37°CIncubationDetects warm-reactive antibodies
    AHG phaseAHG reagentDetects IgG sensitization

    Interpretation

    ResultInterpretation
    No agglutination or hemolysisCompatible
    AgglutinationIncompatible
    HemolysisIncompatible

    Remember: A compatible crossmatch does not guarantee that every possible transfusion reaction will be prevented, but it significantly reduces risk.

    PART VII. BLOOD COMPONENTS AND TRANSFUSION PRACTICES

    44. Blood components and their indications

    Whole blood can be separated into different components to provide the specific blood product required by a patient.

    Master blood component table

    Blood componentMain contentsMajor indication
    Whole bloodRBCs, plasma and plateletsSelected cases of massive blood loss
    Packed RBCs (PRBCs)Concentrated RBCsSymptomatic anemia
    Washed RBCsRBCs with most plasma proteins removedSevere allergic transfusion reactions; IgA deficiency with anti-IgA
    Leukoreduced RBCsRBCs with reduced leukocytesReduce febrile nonhemolytic reactions and CMV transmission risk
    Irradiated RBCsRBCs treated with irradiationPrevention of transfusion-associated graft- versus-host disease
    Frozen RBCsCryopreserved RBCsLong-term storage of rare blood types
    Random donor platelets (RDP)Platelets from one whole-blood donationThrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction
    Single donor platelets (SDP)Platelets collected by apheresisThrombocytopenia; reduces donor exposure
    Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)Plasma containing coagulation factorsMultiple coagulation factor deficiency
    CryoprecipitateFibrinogen, factor VIII, factor XIII, vWF and fibronectinHypofibrinogenemia
    Granulocyte concentrateNeutrophils and other granulocytesSelected severe neutropenia with infection
    Factor concentratesSpecific coagulation factorsFactor deficiencies
    Immune serum globulin (ISG)ImmunoglobulinsImmunodeficiency and selected indications

    Packed RBCs

    Purpose: Increase oxygen-carrying capacity.

    Indications:

    • Symptomatic anemia.
    • Acute blood loss with inadequate oxygen delivery.
    • Selected perioperative and critical-care situations.

    Leukoreduced RBCs

    Leukoreduction removes most donor leukocytes.

    Benefits:

    • Reduces febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reactions.
    • Reduces leukocyte-associated alloimmunization.
    • Reduces risk of transfusion-transmitted CMV, but does not make the product completely CMV-safe in every setting.

    Irradiated blood components

    Irradiation prevents donor T lymphocytes from proliferating.

    Main purpose: Prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GVHD).

    Important indications include:

    • Patients with severe cellular immunodeficiency.
    • Selected hematopoietic stem-cell transplant recipients.
    • Transfusions from blood relatives.
    • HLA-selected cellular components.

    Important distinction:

    • Leukoreduction removes leukocytes.
    • Irradiation inactivates donor lymphocytes.

    They are not interchangeable.

    Washed RBCs

    Washing removes most residual plasma proteins.

    Indications:

    • Recurrent severe allergic transfusion reactions.
    • Selected patients with IgA deficiency and anti-IgA.

    Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)

    FFP contains multiple coagulation factors.

    Indications:

    • Multiple coagulation factor deficiencies.
    • Certain cases of massive transfusion.
    • Selected cases requiring plasma replacement.

    Not indicated simply to increase albumin or expand intravascular volume.

    Cryoprecipitate

    Prepared by thawing FFP at cold temperatures and collecting the precipitated fraction.

    Contains:

    • Fibrinogen.
    • Factor VIII.
    • Factor XIII.
    • von Willebrand factor.
    • Fibronectin.

    Main indication: Hypofibrinogenemia.

    Cryoprecipitate versus FFP

    FeatureFFPCryoprecipitate
    ContentsBroad range of coagulation factorsConcentrated fibrinogen and selected proteins
    Main useMultiple factor deficiencyLow fibrinogen
    VolumeLargerSmaller
    Fibrinogen concentrationLower than cryoprecipitate per unit volumeHigher

    46. Anticoagulants and blood preservation solutions

    Historical development

    YearDevelopment
    1943Loutit and Mollison introduced ACD
    1957CPD was introduced

    ACD versus CPD versus CPDA-1

    ComponentMain function
    CitrateBinds calcium and prevents coagulation
    PhosphateSupports RBC metabolism and pH buffering
    DextroseProvides energy for RBC metabolism
    AdenineSupports ATP production

    Important blood bag solutions

    SolutionComposition / main purpose
    ACDAcid-citrate-dextrose; anticoagulation and preservation
    CPDCitrate-phosphate-dextrose
    CPDA-1Citrate-phosphate-dextrose-adenine; longer storage
    Additive solutionExtends RBC storage and maintains RBC quality

    Storage lesion

    During storage, RBCs undergo biochemical changes collectively called the storage lesion.

    ChangeConsequence
    Decreased pHIncreased acidity
    Decreased glucoseReduced metabolic substrate
    Decreased ATPReduced membrane function
    Decreased 2,3-DPGReduced oxygen release to tissues
    Increased potassiumPotassium leaks into storage solution
    Increased lactateAccumulation of metabolic products
    Decreased RBC deformabilityReduced ability to pass through microcirculation

    ATP and 2,3-DPG

    ATP

    • Maintains RBC membrane integrity.
    • Supports ion pumps.
    • Helps preserve cellular shape and deformability.

    2,3-DPG

    • Binds deoxyhemoglobin.
    • Reduces hemoglobin affinity for oxygen.
    • Facilitates oxygen release to tissues.

    EXAM TIP: Decreased 2,3-DPG causes an increase in hemoglobin's oxygen affinity, shifting the oxygen dissociation curve to the left.

    47. Blood component preparation

    Packed RBC preparation

    Whole blood is centrifuged to separate plasma from RBCs.

    Two main methods:

    • High-speed centrifugation.
    • Light-spin centrifugation.

    Frozen RBC preparation

    Glycerol is used as a cryoprotective agent.

    MethodGlycerol concentrationCharacteristic
    High glycerolApproximately 40%Slow freezing
    Low glycerolApproximately 20%Rapid freezing

    Important: Glycerol protects RBCs from damage during freezing.

    Deglycerolization

    Frozen RBCs must be washed to remove glycerol before transfusion.

    This is accomplished using progressively decreasing concentrations of saline and appropriate washing solutions.

    RBC aliquots

    RBC aliquots are small volumes prepared from a larger unit.

    Applications:

    • Neonatal transfusion.
    • Pediatric transfusion.
    • Patients requiring small-volume transfusions.

    48. Platelet components

    Random donor platelets (RDP) versus single donor platelets (SDP)

    FeatureRDPSDP
    SourceWhole-blood donationApheresis
    Donor exposureMultiple donors may be requiredUsually one donor
    Platelet yieldLower per unitHigher per collection
    HLA alloimmunizationMore donor exposuresReduced donor exposure
    Main useThrombocytopeniaThrombocytopenia

    Platelet storage

    • Stored at 20–24°C.
    • Continuous gentle agitation.
    • Usually five days under the standard described in the source.

    Platelet apheresis

    Apheresis selectively collects a desired blood component while returning the remaining components to the donor.

    Type of apheresisMain component collected
    PlateletpheresisPlatelets
    ErythrocytapheresisRBCs
    LeukapheresisWBCs
    PlasmapheresisPlasma

    Important platelet donor criteria from the source

    • Platelet count should generally be at least 150 × 10³/µL.
    • Donors should avoid aspirin before donation according to the required deferral interval.
    • Platelet collection should follow applicable donor eligibility criteria.

    49. Blood donation

    Types of blood donation

    TypeDescription
    Allogeneic donationBlood donated for another person
    Autologous donationBlood donated for the donor's own future use
    Directed donationDonation intended for a specific recipient
    Designated donationDonation intended for a specified patient
    Preoperative autologous donationBlood collected before an anticipated surgery

    Allogeneic donor eligibility

    The source lists the following general criteria:

    ParameterSource criterion
    AgeAt least 17 years
    TemperatureApproximately 37.5°C or below
    Pulse50–100 bpm
    Systolic BP180 mmHg or below
    Diastolic BP100 mmHg or below
    HemoglobinAt least 12.5 g/dL
    HematocritAt least 38% or 0.38 L/L
    WeightAt least 50 kg
    General conditionAppears healthy

    These are study-guide criteria; actual donor requirements must follow current local blood- service regulations.

    Autologous donation

    The donor receives their own blood.

    Advantages:

    • Avoids exposure to another person's RBC antigens.
    • Useful for selected patients undergoing planned procedures.

    Contraindications listed in the source include:

    • Bacteremia.
    • Significant cardiovascular problems.
    • Pulmonary problems.

    Acute normovolemic hemodilution

    Blood is collected immediately before or during surgery while circulating volume is maintained using appropriate replacement fluids.

    The collected blood can later be returned to the patient.

    50. Blood collection procedure

    The source outlines the following essential steps.

    1. Positively identify the donor.
    2. Inspect the collection bag and equipment.
    3. Perform aseptic skin preparation.
    4. Select an appropriate venipuncture site.
    5. Apply the tourniquet.
    6. Perform venipuncture.
    7. Monitor the donor.
    8. Mix the collection bag periodically.
    9. Collect the required volume.
    10. Properly label and store the unit.
    11. Process blood within the required time.

    Important collection details

    • Blood should be collected using sterile equipment.
    • The anticoagulant must be mixed with the collected blood.
    • The collection bag should be weighed or otherwise monitored to ensure proper volume.
    • Blood intended for component preparation should be processed promptly.

    Donor reactions

    ReactionClinical manifestation
    Vasovagal reactionPallor, sweating, dizziness, syncope
    HyperventilationRapid breathing, lightheadedness
    Citrate toxicityHypocalcemia, tingling, muscle cramps
    Nausea and vomitingGastrointestinal symptoms
    Arterial punctureBright red blood, pulsatile flow, hematoma

    Important: Citrate binds ionized calcium. Citrate toxicity is particularly relevant during large- volume transfusion and apheresis.

    51. Donor deferrals

    Donor deferrals may be permanent, temporary or based on risk assessment.

    Permanent deferral examples

    The source includes:

    • Certain hepatitis infections.
    • HIV infection.
    • Certain high-risk infectious histories.
    • Selected serious medical conditions.

    Temporary deferral examples

    Condition / exposureDeferral concept
    Recent blood exposureTemporary deferral
    Certain vaccinationsDepends on vaccine type
    PregnancyTemporary postpartum deferral
    Recent tattoo or piercingDepends on local regulation and sterile procedure
    Certain infectionsDefer until recovered
    Recent travel to malaria-endemic areasDepends on exposure and applicable guidelines

    Vaccine-related deferral

    Vaccine typeGeneral concept
    Live attenuated vaccineMay require a deferral period
    Inactivated vaccineUsually no deferral if donor is well
    Toxoid vaccineUsually no deferral if donor is well
    Recombinant vaccineUsually no deferral if donor is well

    Important: Do not memorize every historical deferral interval as universally applicable. Current national blood-service policies take precedence.

    52. Processing and testing of donated blood

    Every donated unit must undergo appropriate testing.

    Essential tests

    TestPurpose
    ABO typingDetermines ABO group
    Rh typingDetermines D antigen status
    Antibody screeningDetects unexpected antibodies
    HBsAgDetects hepatitis B surface antigen
    Anti-HBcDetects exposure to hepatitis B
    Anti-HCVDetects hepatitis C antibodies
    HIV screeningDetects HIV infection markers
    Syphilis screeningDetects Treponema pallidum infection
    Malaria screeningUsed according to epidemiologic and regulatory requirements

    Other screening may include tests for relevant transfusion-transmitted infections according to local regulations.

    Transfusion-transmitted syphilis

    The source notes that Treponema pallidum does not survive for prolonged periods in refrigerated stored blood.

    Nevertheless, blood donors must undergo the required syphilis screening.

    53. Blood product selection and transfusion

    Before transfusion

    1. Verify the physician's order.
    2. Confirm patient identity.
    3. Verify ABO and Rh compatibility.
    4. Review antibody screening and crossmatch.
    5. Inspect the blood component.
    6. Verify expiration and unit identification.
    7. Confirm proper administration equipment.

    During transfusion

    The source emphasizes:

    • Positive identification of the patient.
    • Proper venous access.
    • Monitoring vital signs.
    • Close observation during the first 10–15 minutes.
    • Slow initial infusion.
    • Completing transfusion within the appropriate time limit, generally no longer than four hours for a unit of RBCs.

    Important transfusion precautions

    • Do not administer incompatible blood.
    • Use appropriate blood administration sets.
    • Normal saline is the standard compatible solution for routine RBC administration.
    • Do not add medications directly to blood components.
    • Monitor for signs of transfusion reactions.

    Special transfusion procedures

    ProcedurePurpose
    Emergency transfusionProvides blood when waiting for complete compatibility testing is unsafe
    Massive transfusionReplaces large-volume blood loss
    Neonatal RBC transfusionUses specially selected RBC units for neonates
    Intrauterine transfusionTreats severe fetal anemia
    Exchange transfusionReplaces a patient's blood with donor blood

    Exchange transfusion

    Blood is withdrawn and replaced in repeated cycles.

    Clinical applications:

    • Severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.
    • Severe HDFN.
    • Selected hemoglobinopathies.

    54. Blood reissue

    Blood may be considered for reissue only if all required conditions are satisfied.

    The source lists:

    1. The blood container closure must remain intact.
    2. The blood must have been continuously stored at the appropriate temperature.
    3. The attached pilot tube or segment must remain intact.
    4. The unit must not have been outside controlled storage beyond the permitted time.
    5. Records must show that all criteria were met.

    EXAM TIP: A unit that has been improperly stored or whose integrity is compromised must not simply be returned to inventory.

    PART VIII. TRANSFUSION REACTIONS

    55. Classification of transfusion reactions

    Transfusion reactions may be classified according to:

    • Timing: acute or delayed.
    • Mechanism: immune or nonimmune.
    • Clinical manifestation: hemolytic, allergic, pulmonary, circulatory or infectious.

    Master transfusion reaction table

    ReactionMechanismOnsetMain manifestation
    Acute hemolytic transfusion reactionABO incompatibility; complement-mediated hemolysisDuring or shortly after transfusionFever, chills, hypotension, hemoglobinuria
    Delayed hemolytic transfusion reactionAnamnestic alloantibody responseDays to weeksFalling hemoglobin, jaundice
    Febrile nonhemolytic reactionCytokines or leukocyte antibodiesDuring or within hoursFever and chills
    Allergic reactionHypersensitivity to plasma proteinsDuring or shortly afterUrticaria, itching
    Anaphylactic reactionSevere systemic hypersensitivityRapidHypotension, bronchospasm, shock
    TRALIImmune-mediated pulmonary injuryDuring or within 6 hoursAcute hypoxemia, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema
    TACOCirculatory volume overloadDuring or within 12 hoursDyspnea, pulmonary edema, hypertension
    Septic transfusion reactionBacterial contaminationDuring or shortly afterHigh fever, hypotension, shock
    TA-GVHDDonor T lymphocytes attack recipient tissueDays to weeksFever, rash, diarrhea, liver dysfunction, pancytopenia
    Hypotensive transfusion reactionBradykinin-related mechanism in some settingsDuring transfusionSudden hypotension

    56. Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR)

    AHTR is a serious immune-mediated reaction most commonly associated with ABO incompatibility.

    Pathophysiology

    1. Incompatible donor RBCs enter the recipient.
    2. Recipient antibodies bind donor RBC antigens.
    3. Complement is activated.
    4. RBCs undergo intravascular hemolysis.
    5. Free hemoglobin is released.
    6. Inflammatory mediators contribute to hypotension, shock and organ injury.

    Clinical manifestations

    • Fever.
    • Chills.
    • Flushing.
    • Back or flank pain.
    • Hypotension.
    • Hemoglobinuria.
    • Disseminated intravascular coagulation.
    • Acute kidney injury.

    Laboratory findings

    TestExpected finding
    DATMay be positive
    Plasma free hemoglobinIncreased
    HemoglobinuriaMay be present
    LDHIncreased
    Indirect bilirubinIncreased
    HaptoglobinDecreased
    HemoglobinMay decrease

    Immediate management

    1. STOP the transfusion immediately.
    2. Maintain IV access using normal saline and new tubing.
    3. Verify patient and blood unit identification.
    4. Notify the physician and blood bank.
    5. Send post-transfusion blood and urine specimens as required.
    6. Return the blood unit and administration set.
    7. Perform a transfusion reaction investigation.

    Never restart a suspected incompatible transfusion.

    57. Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR)

    A DHTR results from an anamnestic immune response against a previously encountered RBC antigen.

    Mechanism

    1. Patient previously develops an alloantibody.
    2. Antibody concentration falls below detection.
    3. Patient receives RBCs bearing the corresponding antigen.
    4. Memory B cells rapidly produce antibodies.
    5. Transfused RBCs are destroyed.

    Common antibody associations

    • Kidd: anti-Jka, anti-Jkb.
    • Duffy: anti-Fya, anti-Fyb.
    • Rh: anti-E, anti-c.
    • Kell: anti-K.

    High-yield: Kidd antibodies are notorious for evanescence and delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions.

    Clinical findings

    • Unexplained decline in hemoglobin.
    • Jaundice.
    • Increased indirect bilirubin.
    • Increased LDH.
    • Positive DAT in some cases.

    58. Febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR)

    Usually associated with recipient antibodies against donor leukocytes or inflammatory cytokines accumulated during storage.

    Manifestations

    • Fever.
    • Chills.
    • Rigors.
    • No evidence of hemolysis.

    Prevention

    - Leukoreduced blood components.

    Important: Always exclude acute hemolytic reaction and bacterial contamination before diagnosing FNHTR.

    59. Allergic and anaphylactic reactions

    Allergic reaction

    Usually caused by hypersensitivity to plasma proteins.

    Manifestations:

    • Urticaria.
    • Itching.
    • Flushing.
    • Mild allergic symptoms.

    Management depends on severity and clinical assessment.

    Anaphylactic reaction

    A severe systemic reaction.

    May involve:

    • Severe hypotension.
    • Bronchospasm.
    • Respiratory distress.
    • Angioedema.
    • Shock.

    A classic association is IgA-deficient recipients with anti-IgA antibodies.

    Prevention: Washed cellular components or other specially selected products may be indicated in appropriately evaluated patients.

    Allergic versus anaphylactic reactions

    FeatureAllergicAnaphylactic
    SeverityUsually mildSevere
    UrticariaCommonMay occur
    HypotensionUncommonCommon
    BronchospasmUncommonMay be severe
    ShockRarePossible
    Plasma proteinsOften implicatedMay involve IgA-related hypersensitivity

    60. TRALI versus TACO

    This is one of the most frequently tested transfusion-reaction comparisons.

    FeatureTRALITACO
    Full nameTransfusion-related acute lung injuryTransfusion-associated circulatory overload
    MechanismPulmonary endothelial injuryExcess circulatory volume
    Type of pulmonary edemaNoncardiogenicCardiogenic / hydrostatic
    OnsetDuring or within 6 hoursDuring or within 12 hours
    Blood pressureOften hypotension or normalOften hypertension
    JVPUsually not elevatedMay be elevated
    BNPOften not markedly elevatedMay be elevated
    DiureticsNot routinely beneficial; supportive careUsually beneficial
    Main treatmentSupportive respiratory careDiuresis and fluid management

    Memory aid:

    • TRALI = Lung injury.
    • TACO = Too much volume.

    61. Other transfusion reactions

    Bacterial contamination / septic transfusion reaction

    Caused by contaminated blood components.

    Potential organisms:

    • Staphylococcus epidermidis.
    • Staphylococcus aureus.
    • Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
    • Yersinia enterocolitica.

    Important: Platelets are particularly susceptible because they are stored at room temperature.

    TA-GVHD

    Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease occurs when viable donor lymphocytes attack recipient tissues.

    Clinical findings:

    • Fever.
    • Skin rash.
    • Diarrhea.
    • Liver dysfunction.
    • Bone marrow failure.
    • Pancytopenia.

    Prevention: Irradiation of cellular blood components.

    Massive transfusion complications

    ComplicationMechanism
    Citrate toxicityCalcium binding
    HypocalcemiaReduced ionized calcium
    HyperkalemiaPotassium leakage from stored RBCs
    HypothermiaAdministration of cold components
    Dilutional coagulopathyDilution of coagulation factors and platelets
    Acid-base disturbancesChanges in metabolic and transfusion physiology

    Transfusion reaction investigation

    The source provides the following work-up:

    1. Clerical check.
    2. Visual inspection of pre- and post-transfusion specimens.
    3. Direct antiglobulin test.
    4. Repeat ABO/Rh typing and compatibility testing.
    5. Bilirubin, hemoglobin and hematocrit assessment.

    Additional testing may include:

    • Plasma-free hemoglobin.
    • LDH.
    • Haptoglobin.
    • Urinalysis.
    • Blood cultures if bacterial contamination is suspected.

    63. Kell blood group system

    The Kell system is highly clinically significant.

    Characteristics

    • Antigens are proteins.
    • The K antigen is highly immunogenic.
    • Kell antigens are generally destroyed by DTT and AET.
    • Kell antibodies are commonly IgG.
    • Kell antibodies can cause HTR and HDFN.

    Important Kell antigens

    • K.
    • k.
    • Kpa.
    • Kpb.
    • Jsa.
    • Jsb.

    High-yield: Anti-K is clinically significant and can suppress fetal erythropoiesis, contributing to fetal anemia.

    64. Kidd blood group system

    Important antigens

    • Jka.
    • Jkb.

    Characteristics

    • Kidd antibodies can activate complement.
    • They are often weak and may become undetectable.
    • They can cause delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions.
    • They are clinically significant.

    Most important association: Anti-Jka and anti-Jkb are classic causes of delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions.

    65. Duffy blood group system

    Important antigens

    • Fya.
    • Fyb.

    Characteristics

    • Antibodies are usually IgG.
    • They are clinically significant.
    • They may be destroyed by enzyme treatment.
    • Duffy antigens act as receptors for certain Plasmodium vivax strains.

    High-yield association: Duffy-null phenotype is associated with resistance to many P. vivax strains.

    66. MNS blood group system

    Important antigens:

    • M.
    • N.
    • S.
    • s.
    • U.

    Characteristics

    AntibodyTypical characteristics
    Anti-MUsually IgM; cold-reactive; may be clinically significant if reactive at 37°C
    Anti-NUsually IgM; generally insignificant
    Anti-SUsually IgG; clinically significant
    Anti-sUsually IgG; clinically significant
    Anti-UUsually IgG; may cause severe HTR and HDFN

    Important: Anti-M can occasionally be IgG and clinically significant, especially when reactive at 37°C.

    67. P1PK and GLOB blood group systems

    P1PK system

    Includes:

    • P1.
    • Pk.

    Anti-P1 is generally:

    • Naturally occurring.
    • IgM.
    • Cold-reactive.
    • Usually not clinically significant.

    P antigen and paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria

    The Donath-Landsteiner antibody is typically a biphasic IgG anti-P antibody.

    It binds RBCs in the cold and causes complement-mediated hemolysis upon warming.

    Clinical association

    Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH).

    I and i antigens

    AntigenMain characteristic
    IAdult RBC antigen
    iMore prominent on neonatal RBCs

    Anti-I is associated with cold agglutinin disease.

    Anti-i may be associated with certain infections, particularly infectious mononucleosis.

    68. Duffy, Kidd and Kell: comparison for examinations

    CharacteristicKellDuffyKidd
    Major antigensK, kFya, FybJka, Jkb
    Antibody typeIgGIgGIgG
    Reactivity37°C37°C37°C
    ComplementUsually not a major featureUsually not a major featureCan activate complement
    Enzyme effectDestroyed by DTTDestroyed by enzymesEnhanced by enzymes
    Main associationSevere HDFN; suppressed erythropoiesisP. vivax resistanceDelayed HTR
    Clinical significanceSignificantSignificantSignificant

    69. Lutheran blood group system

    Important antigens:

    • Lua.
    • Lub.

    Characteristics:

    • Lutheran antibodies may be IgG or IgM.
    • Anti-Lua is often naturally occurring and relatively insignificant.
    • Anti-Lub can be clinically significant.
    • Lub is more common than Lua.

    70. Other rare blood group systems

    SystemImportant details
    DiegoDia and Dib; Dia has population-specific significance and may be clinically significant
    ColtonCoa and Cob; antibodies can cause HDFN
    DombrockDoa and Dob; antibodies may be difficult to identify
    GerbichGe antigens; associated with glycophorin-related RBC structures

    McLeod syndrome

    Associated with the absence or reduced expression of Kx antigen.

    Characteristics:

    • Acanthocytosis.
    • Chronic hemolysis.
    • Neuromuscular abnormalities.
    • Reduced Kell antigen expression.

    PNH and CD55/CD59

    Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria results from acquired PIGA mutations affecting GPI- anchor synthesis.

    This causes loss of GPI-anchored complement regulatory proteins, particularly:

    • CD55.
    • CD59.

    The RBCs become vulnerable to complement-mediated destruction.

    High-yield: PNH = loss of CD55 and CD59 → complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis.

    PART X. CLINICAL IMMUNOLOGY AND SEROLOGICAL DIAGNOSTICS

    71. Tumor immunology

    Tumors arise from abnormal cellular growth and may express antigens that can be detected through immunologic and serologic methods.

    Types of tumors

    TypeOrigin
    CarcinomaEpithelial tissue
    SarcomaMesenchymal / connective tissue
    LeukemiaHematopoietic cells
    LymphomaLymphoid tissue
    MyelomaPlasma cells

    Tumor markers

    Tumor markers are substances produced by tumor cells or by the body in response to malignancy.

    They can assist in:

    • Screening selected high-risk populations.
    • Diagnosis.
    • Prognosis.
    • Monitoring treatment.
    • Detecting recurrence.

    Important: Most tumor markers are not sufficiently specific to be used alone for cancer diagnosis.

    Master tumor marker table

    Tumor markerMajor association
    AFPHepatocellular carcinoma; yolk sac tumors
    CEAColorectal cancer; other gastrointestinal malignancies
    CA-125Epithelial ovarian cancer
    CA 15-3Breast cancer monitoring
    CA 19-9Pancreatic and biliary tract cancers
    CA 72-4Gastric and certain ovarian cancers
    CA 27-29Breast cancer monitoring
    PSAProstate cancer
    β-hCGGestational trophoblastic disease; germ-cell tumors
    CalcitoninMedullary thyroid carcinoma
    ThyroglobulinDifferentiated thyroid cancer monitoring
    CYFRA 21-1Non-small-cell lung cancer, especially squamous cell carcinoma
    NSESmall-cell lung cancer and neuroendocrine tumors

    Other tumor-associated markers

    MarkerClinical significance
    BRAF mutationsTargetable mutations in certain malignancies
    BCR-ABLChronic myeloid leukemia
    HER2/neuBreast and gastric cancer
    BRCA1/BRCA2Hereditary breast and ovarian cancer susceptibility
    ER/PRHormone receptor status in breast cancer

    Tumor marker interpretation

    Remember: A tumor marker may be elevated in a benign condition or inflammatory disease. A normal tumor marker does not completely exclude malignancy.

    72. Hypersensitivity reactions

    Hypersensitivity refers to an exaggerated or inappropriate immune response that causes tissue injury.

    There are four major types according to the Gell and Coombs classification.

    Master hypersensitivity table

    TypeMain mechanismMajor immune mediatorOnsetClassic examples
    Type IImmediate hypersensitivityIgE, mast cells, basophilsMinutesAnaphylaxis, allergic rhinitis, asthma
    Type IIAntibody-mediated cytotoxicity or receptor dysfunctionIgG, IgM, complementHours to daysAIHA, HDFN, Goodpasture
    Type IIIImmune-complex depositionIgG, IgM, complementHours to daysSLE, serum sickness, Arthus reaction
    Type IVDelayed, cell-mediated hypersensitivityT lymphocytes48–72 hours or longerContact dermatitis, tuberculin reaction

    Type I: Immediate hypersensitivity

    Mechanism:

    1. First exposure to allergen.
    2. Th2 response stimulates B-cell class switching to IgE.
    3. IgE binds to FcεRI receptors on mast cells and basophils.
    1. Subsequent allergen exposure cross-links IgE.
    2. Degranulation occurs.
    3. Histamine and other mediators are released.

    Important mediators

    MediatorEffect
    HistamineVasodilation, increased permeability, bronchoconstriction
    LeukotrienesBronchoconstriction and increased mucus production
    ProstaglandinsInflammation and bronchoconstriction
    TryptaseMarker of mast-cell activation
    Eosinophil chemotactic factorsRecruit eosinophils

    Type I examples

    • Allergic rhinitis.
    • Urticaria.
    • Atopic asthma.
    • Food allergy.
    • Anaphylaxis.

    Type II: Antibody-mediated hypersensitivity

    IgG or IgM binds to cell-surface or extracellular matrix antigens.

    Possible mechanisms:

    • Complement-mediated cell destruction.
    • Opsonization and phagocytosis.
    • Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
    • Receptor stimulation or inhibition.
    DiseaseTarget
    Autoimmune hemolytic anemiaRBC antigens
    Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newbornFetal RBC antigens
    Goodpasture syndromeGlomerular and alveolar basement membrane
    Myasthenia gravisAcetylcholine receptor
    Graves diseaseTSH receptor
    Transfusion reactionDonor RBC antigens

    DAT: Commonly used in the laboratory investigation of antibody-mediated RBC sensitization.

    Type III: Immune-complex hypersensitivity

    Antigen-antibody complexes form and deposit in tissues.

    This activates complement and recruits inflammatory cells, causing tissue injury.

    Examples:

    • Systemic lupus erythematosus.
    • Serum sickness.
    • Arthus reaction.
    • Certain forms of glomerulonephritis.

    Type IV: Delayed hypersensitivity

    Mediated by T lymphocytes rather than antibodies.

    Mechanisms:

    • Th1 cytokine release.
    • Macrophage activation.
    • Cytotoxic T-cell activity.

    Examples:

    • Tuberculin skin test.
    • Allergic contact dermatitis.
    • Certain drug reactions.
    • Granulomatous inflammation.

    Type IV subdivisions

    SubtypeMechanism
    IVaTh1 cells and macrophages
    IVbTh2 cells and eosinophils
    IVcCytotoxic T cells
    IVdT-cell-mediated neutrophilic inflammation

    Hypersensitivity memory aid

    • Type I = IgE / Immediate.
    • Type II = IgG or IgM / Cytotoxic.
    • Type III = Immune complexes.
    • Type IV = T cells / Delayed.

    Group A Streptococcus

    Streptococcus pyogenes is associated with:

    • Impetigo.
    • Acute rheumatic fever.

    75. Corynebacterium diphtheriae

    Causes diphtheria through the production of diphtheria toxin.

    Clinical features

    • Sore throat.
    • Fever.
    • Gray pseudomembrane.
    • Cervical lymphadenopathy.
    • Potential myocarditis and neurologic complications.

    Laboratory diagnosis

    • Culture.
    • Identification of C. diphtheriae.
    • Toxin detection.
    • PCR for toxin genes.
    • Elek test for toxin production.

    Elek test: Immunodiffusion-based test used to demonstrate toxin production.

    76. Mycoplasma pneumoniae

    A common cause of atypical pneumonia, sometimes called walking pneumonia.

    Characteristics

    • Lacks a cell wall.
    • Not susceptible to antibiotics that target cell-wall synthesis.
    • Can produce cold agglutinins.
    • Commonly causes respiratory infection.

    Laboratory diagnosis

    MethodPrinciple
    Cold agglutinin testDetects cold-reactive antibodies
    ELISADetects specific antibodies
    PCRDetects organism DNA
    CultureSpecialized culture techniques

    Cold agglutinins

    Antibodies, commonly IgM, may agglutinate RBCs at low temperatures.

    The classic association is anti-I.

    Important: Cold agglutinin testing is not sufficiently specific to serve as the definitive modern diagnostic test for M. pneumoniae.

    77. Rickettsial infections

    Rickettsiae are small, obligate intracellular gram-negative bacteria.

    Important organisms and diseases

    OrganismDisease
    Rickettsia rickettsiiRocky Mountain spotted fever
    Rickettsia prowazekiiEpidemic typhus
    Rickettsia typhiEndemic typhus

    Weil-Felix test

    The Weil-Felix test is a historical heterophile agglutination test based on cross-reactivity between Rickettsial antibodies and Proteus antigens.

    Proteus strains

    Proteus antigenAssociated infection
    OX-19Certain typhus-group rickettsioses
    OX-2Spotted fever group rickettsioses
    OX-KScrub typhus

    Principle

    Patient serum is tested against Proteus OX antigens.

    Agglutination indicates possible cross-reacting antibodies.

    Limitations:

    • Low sensitivity.
    • Low specificity.
    • False-positive reactions.
    • False-negative reactions.

    More reliable diagnostic methods

    • Indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA).
    • PCR.
    • Appropriate paired serologic testing.

    78. Salmonella and Widal test

    Salmonella Typhi

    Causes typhoid fever.

    The organism has important antigens:

    AntigenMeaning
    O antigenSomatic antigen; part of LPS
    H antigenFlagellar antigen
    Vi antigenCapsular antigen

    Widal test

    The Widal test detects antibodies against Salmonella O and H antigens.

    Principle

    Patient serum is mixed with standardized Salmonella antigen suspensions.

    If specific antibodies are present, visible agglutination occurs.

    Antigen comparison

    AntigenLocationCharacteristics
    OCell wall / LPSSomatic antigen; generally more associated with early antibody response
    HFlagellaFlagellar antigen; often associated with later or persistent antibody response
    ViCapsuleMay be associated with virulence and carrier detection

    Widal interpretation

    The source provides this grading scheme:

    ReactionApproximate interpretation
    0No agglutination
    +125% agglutination
    +250% agglutination
    +375% agglutination
    +4100% agglutination

    The source also notes that a single titer is not considered positive unless it reaches a designated significant threshold; this threshold must be locally established.

    Widal limitations

    1. Previous infection may produce persistent antibodies.
    2. Vaccination can affect antibody levels.
    3. Cross-reactivity may occur.
    4. Endemic exposure affects baseline titers.
    5. Early infection may yield negative results.
    6. Interpretation of a single titer is unreliable.

    Best practice: Blood culture is the preferred diagnostic method for typhoid fever when available. Paired serologic titers may provide additional information, but Widal should not be treated as a definitive standalone test.

    79. Coagglutination test

    Coagglutination uses bacteria, commonly Staphylococcus aureus, as carrier particles.

    The protein A of S. aureus binds the Fc portion of IgG.

    This leaves the Fab portions available to bind the target antigen.

    Principle

    1. Protein A binds antibody Fc regions.
    2. Antibody Fab regions remain available.
    3. The antibody binds its corresponding antigen.
    4. Visible agglutination occurs.

    Applications:

    • Identification of certain bacterial antigens.
    • Historical use in microbial identification.

    Important: Protein A binds the Fc region of IgG, allowing the Fab regions to remain available for antigen recognition.

    80. Lyme disease

    Caused by Borrelia burgdorferi and transmitted by infected ticks.

    Clinical stages

    StageCharacteristics
    Early localizedErythema migrans
    Early disseminatedMultiple lesions, neurologic and cardiac manifestations
    Late disseminatedArthritis and other persistent manifestations

    Laboratory diagnosis

    • Enzyme immunoassay (EIA).
    • Immunoblotting when indicated.
    • Modified two-tier testing using appropriate immunoassays.
    • PCR in selected clinical specimens.

    High-yield: Erythema migrans in an appropriate exposure setting is a clinical diagnosis and should not be ruled out by an early negative antibody test.

    Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum.

    VDRL

    Reagent components:

    • Cardiolipin.
    • Lecithin.
    • Cholesterol.

    VDRL procedure

    1. Patient serum is placed on a slide.
    2. Standardized antigen suspension is added.
    3. The mixture is rotated.
    4. Flocculation is observed microscopically.

    RPR

    The RPR test is a modified VDRL test.

    It uses carbon particles to make the flocculation reaction visible macroscopically.

    VDRLRPR

    FTA-ABS

    Uses fluorescently labeled anti-human immunoglobulin to detect antibodies attached to treponemal antigens.

    TP-PA

    Uses gelatin particles coated with T. pallidum antigens.

    If specific antibodies are present, particle agglutination occurs.

    Interpretation

    NontreponemalTreponemalPossible interpretation

    PositiveNegativeBiological false-positive nontreponemal result is possible

    NegativeNegativeNo serologic evidence, but early infection may still be possible

    Prozone in syphilis testing

    Very high antibody concentrations may prevent optimal flocculation.

    If clinical suspicion is high despite a negative test, serial dilution may be necessary.

    Important: The prozone phenomenon can cause false-negative RPR or VDRL results.

    Hemagglutination inhibition

    This method detects antibodies that inhibit virus-induced RBC agglutination.

    Principle:

    1. Virus is mixed with patient serum.
    2. Specific antibodies bind viral hemagglutinin.
    3. RBCs are added.
    4. If antibodies inhibit hemagglutination, RBCs form a compact button rather than a diffuse lattice.

    PART XII. ADDITIONAL HIGH-YIELD LABORATORY METHODS

    86. Immunofluorescence

    Immunofluorescence uses fluorescently labeled antibodies to detect antigens or antibodies.

    Direct versus indirect immunofluorescence

    FeatureDirect immunofluorescenceIndirect immunofluorescence
    DetectsAntigen in patient specimenAntibody in patient serum
    Labeled reagentFluorescent primary antibodyFluorescent secondary antibody
    StepsFewerMore
    SensitivityGenerally lowerGenerally higher due to signal amplification
    ApplicationTissue antigen detectionAutoantibody testing

    Direct immunofluorescence

    1. Patient tissue is collected.
    1. Fluorescently labeled specific antibody is added.
    2. Antibody binds to target antigen.
    3. Excess reagent is washed away.
    4. Fluorescence is observed.

    Indirect immunofluorescence

    1. Patient serum is added to antigen-containing substrate.
    2. Patient antibodies bind to antigen.
    3. Unbound antibodies are washed away.
    4. Fluorescently labeled anti-human immunoglobulin is added.
    5. Fluorescence is observed.

    Important applications

    • ANA testing.
    • Autoimmune disease investigation.
    • Infectious disease diagnosis.
    • Detection of tissue-bound immunoglobulins.
    • Certain parasitic infections.

    87. Radioimmunoassay (RIA)

    RIA is an immunoassay that uses radioactive labels to measure antigen or antibody.

    The source attributes its development to Rosalyn Yalow.

    Principle

    In a classical competitive RIA:

    1. A fixed amount of radiolabeled antigen is mixed with patient sample.
    2. Labeled and unlabeled antigen compete for a limited number of antibody-binding sites.
    3. The bound and free fractions are separated.
    4. Radioactivity is measured.

    Important: In competitive RIA, greater analyte concentration generally means less radiolabeled antigen is bound.

    RIA versus ELISA

    FeatureRIAELISA
    LabelRadioisotopeEnzyme
    DetectionRadiation measurementColorimetric or other enzyme-generated signal
    SensitivityHighHigh
    Main disadvantageRadiation hazards and wasteEnzyme/reagent interference
    ApplicationHormones and other analytesAntigens and antibodies

    Inhibition immunofluorescence

    In this method, unlabeled antigen competes with labeled antigen or antibody for available binding sites.

    A reduction or absence of fluorescence may indicate the presence of the target substance.

    Particle-counting immunoassay (PACI)

    Particle-counting immunoassay measures residual particles following antigen-antibody interactions.

    The source describes the use of an optical particle counter, where particles pass through a laser beam and are detected.

    Important principle: Large particles and very small particles may be excluded or handled according to the instrument's detection thresholds.

    PART XVIII. IMPORTANT CORRECTIONS AND CLARIFICATIONS

    There are a few areas in the uploaded reviewer that are worth understanding more precisely instead of memorizing without context.

    TopicImportant clarification
    IgG complement activationIgG1 and IgG3 activate complement efficiently; not every IgG subclass does so equally
    IgG4Does not efficiently activate the classical complement pathway
    C3a and C5aBoth are anaphylatoxins, but C5a is the more potent chemotactic factor
    Job syndromeClassically associated with STAT3 dysfunction and impaired Th17- mediated host defense
    Chronic granulomatous diseaseDefective NADPH oxidase and oxidative burst
    ABO antibodiesGroup O individuals may have clinically significant IgG anti-A,B
    Bombay phenotypeCannot receive ordinary group O RBCs because of anti-H
    Secretor geneFUT2 determines secretor status; FUT1 is primarily responsible for RBC H antigen expression
    Rh antibodiesUsually immune IgG, not naturally occurring
    DTTDestroys Kell antigens as well as disrupting IgM antibodies
    Enzyme treatmentCan enhance some antigen reactions and destroy others; it should not be used in isolation to identify antibodies
    Complement fixationPositive = absence of hemolysis
    DATDetects IgG and/or complement already bound to RBCs in vivo
    IATDetects antibodies that sensitize RBCs in vitro
    Widal testCannot definitively diagnose typhoid from a single titer
    Weil-FelixHistorical test with limited sensitivity and specificity

    PART XIX. FINAL ONE-PAGE MEMORY SHEET

    ISBB MTAP 100 — RAPID RECALL

    IMMUNOLOGY

    • Neutrophil = acute bacterial infection.
    • Eosinophil = parasites/allergy.
    • Basophil = histamine.
    • Monocyte = largest circulating WBC.
    • Kupffer = liver.
    • Microglia = CNS.
    • NK = CD16/CD56.
    • CD3 = T cell.
    • CD19/CD20 = B cell.
    • CD34 = stem cell.
    • CD45 = leukocytes.
    • MHC I = CD8.
    • MHC II = CD4.
    • IL-1 = fever.
    • IL-6 = CRP.
    • IL-8 = neutrophil chemotaxis.
    • IL-12 = NK/Th1.
    • IL-5 = eosinophils.

    IMMUNOGLOBULINS

    • IgG = placenta, secondary response.
    • IgM = primary response, best agglutination.
    • IgA = mucosal immunity.
    • IgE = allergy.
    • IgD = B-cell receptor.
    • Papain = 2 Fab + Fc.
    • Pepsin = F(ab')₂.

    COMPLEMENT

    • C3b = opsonization.
    • C3a/C5a = anaphylatoxins.
    • C5a = strongest chemotaxis.
    • C5b–C9 = MAC.
    • C3 deficiency = severe infections.
    • C5–C9 deficiency = Neisseria.
    • C1-INH deficiency = hereditary angioedema.
    • CD55/CD59 loss = PNH.

    SEROLOGY

    • Agglutination = particulate antigen.
    • Precipitation = soluble antigen.
    • Prozone = antibody excess.
    • Postzone = antigen excess.
    • Equivalence = optimal ratio.
    • Nephelometry = scattered light.
    • Turbidimetry = transmitted light blocked.
    • CFT positive = NO hemolysis.
    • Southern = DNA.
    • Northern = RNA.
    • Western = protein.
    • PCR = denaturation, annealing, extension.

    BLOOD BANKING

    • Forward typing = RBC antigen.
    • Reverse typing = serum antibody.
    • Group O = most H antigen.
    • A antigen = N-acetylgalactosamine.
    • B antigen = galactose.
    • Bombay = no H antigen, anti-H.
    • Rh = protein antigen.
    • Anti-D = IgG.
    • DAT = in vivo.
    • IAT = in vitro.
    • Major crossmatch = donor RBC + recipient serum.
    • Kidd = delayed HTR.
    • Kell = destroyed by DTT.
    • Duffy = destroyed by enzymes.
    • RhIG = prevention of anti-D sensitization.

    TRANSFUSION

    • RBCs = 1–6°C.
    • Platelets = 20–24°C.
    • FFP = multiple coagulation factors.
    • Cryoprecipitate = fibrinogen.
    • Irradiation = prevent TA-GVHD.
    • Leukoreduction = reduce leukocyte-related complications.
    • AHTR = ABO incompatibility.
    • DHTR = anamnestic alloantibody.
    • TRALI = noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.
    • TACO = circulatory overload.

    INFECTIOUS DISEASES

    • Widal = Salmonella O/H.
    • Weil-Felix = Proteus OX.
    • ASO = streptolysin O.
    • Syphilis screening = RPR/VDRL.
    • Syphilis confirmation = TP-PA/FTA-ABS.
    • EBV = heterophile antibodies.
    • Dengue = NS1, IgM, PCR.
    • HBV window period = IgM anti-HBc.
    • HCV active infection = HCV RNA.
    • Lyme = Borrelia burgdorferi.
    • Malaria = thick and thin smears.

    Recommended reference books for deeper study

    These are the major references I recommend using alongside your lecture reviewer.

    1. Harmening – Modern Blood Banking and Transfusion Practices. Particularly useful for ABO/Rh typing, antibody identification, blood group systems, compatibility testing, component preparation and transfusion reactions.
    1. Stevens – Clinical Immunology and Serology. Useful for immunologic mechanisms, hypersensitivity, autoimmunity, infectious disease serology, immunoassays and complement.
    2. Turgeon – Immunology and Serology in Laboratory Medicine. Useful for antigen- antibody reactions, diagnostic principles, serologic testing, immunoglobulins and clinical applications.

    For the blood banking portion, prioritize Harmening. For immune mechanisms and serologic principles, prioritize Stevens and Turgeon.

    My recommended study priority:

    PriorityTopicsWhy
    ABO, Rh, antibody screening, identification and crossmatchingCore transfusion medicine
    Blood group systems and clinically significant antibodiesCommonly tested in identification panels
    DAT, IAT, AHG, enzymes and enhancement mediaEssential laboratory principles
    Transfusion reactions and blood componentsImportant clinical applications
    Immunoglobulins, complement and hypersensitivityCore immunology
    Cytokines, chemokines and CD markersImportant memorization topics
    Serologic reactions and assay principlesFrequently tested distinctions
    Infectious disease serology and tumor markersImportant diagnostic associations

    One final examination reminder: Do not just memorize whether a test is positive or negative. Memorize its specimen, reagent, principle, reaction phase, positive indicator, clinical application and limitations. Those six elements will help you solve both straightforward identification questions and complicated situational questions.
